items.prompt: Why has the flight been delayed?
items.audio:
Good morning, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to Tashkent International Airport. This is an important announcement for all passengers travelling on the flight to Samarkand. Because of thick fog that covered the city early this morning, our aircraft arrived late from Moscow, and the departure has been delayed by two hours. The flight was due to leave at eight thirty, but the new departure time is half past ten. We are very sorry for the inconvenience, and we thank you for your patience.

While you wait, the airline would like to offer every passenger a free breakfast. Please take the voucher that our staff are giving out at gate number twelve and show it at the Blue Garden cafe on the first floor. The voucher is valid for one hot drink and one sandwich or pastry. Passengers who are travelling with small children can also use the quiet family room next to gate fourteen, where there are comfortable chairs, toys and a small kitchen for warming baby food.

If you have a connecting flight, please do not worry. Our service desk, which is located near the main entrance, will help you change your ticket without any extra payment. The desk is open from six in the morning until midnight, and the staff speak Uzbek, Russian and English. Passengers who decide that they no longer want to travel today may ask for a full refund, but they must do it before nine o'clock.

We also remind you that the weather is expected to improve soon. The forecast says that the fog will disappear by nine, and the sun will come out later in the morning. Please keep an eye on the information screens, because the gate may change at short notice. Boarding will begin forty minutes before departure, and we ask all passengers to have their passports and boarding passes ready. Remember that each passenger may carry one small bag into the cabin, and heavier bags must go into the hold. The flight to Samarkand takes about fifty minutes, and the captain, Mr Karimov, promises a smooth journey. Thank you once again, and we wish you a pleasant stay at our airport.

items.prompt: Who will Dilnoza travel with?
items.audio:
Dilnoza wanted to spend a long weekend in Istanbul with her sister Malika, so on Monday evening she telephoned a small hotel near the Blue Mosque. A friendly man called Mehmet answered the phone and asked how he could help. Dilnoza explained that she needed a double room with two separate beds for three nights, from the fourteenth to the seventeenth of May. Mehmet checked his computer and said that he had one room left on the third floor with a view of the sea.

Dilnoza asked about the price. Mehmet answered that the room cost ninety euros a night, and breakfast was included. She thought that was a little expensive, so she asked whether there was a cheaper room. He said that a room without a view on the ground floor cost seventy euros, but it was next to the kitchen and could be noisy in the morning. Dilnoza decided that she preferred to pay more and sleep well, so she chose the room with the sea view.

Then she asked some practical questions. How far was the hotel from the airport? Mehmet explained that it was about forty kilometres away, and that the hotel could send a car for twenty-five euros. A taxi from the street would be cheaper, but the driver might choose a longer road. Dilnoza liked the idea of a safe car waiting for them, because their plane would land very late at night, at a quarter to midnight. Mehmet promised that the driver would hold a sign with her name.

Finally, Mehmet asked for her details. She spelled her name slowly, gave her email address and said that she would pay by credit card. He told her that she could cancel the booking free of charge until a week before arrival. After that, the hotel would keep the price of the first night. Dilnoza thanked him warmly, and Mehmet said that he would send a confirmation message within ten minutes. When she put the phone down, she called Malika at once to share the good news. Her sister was delighted and immediately began to make a list of the places they wanted to see, including the Grand Bazaar and a boat trip on the Bosphorus.

items.prompt: How long does the trip from Tashkent to Bukhara take?
items.audio:
Welcome to Travel Talk on Radio Silk Road. I am your host, Aziza, and today I want to speak about the joys of travelling by train. Many people think that trains are slow and old fashioned, but I have changed my mind this year after a journey from Tashkent to Bukhara on the high-speed train. The trip takes only about three hours, and the carriages are clean, quiet and very comfortable.

Let me tell you about my own journey. I arrived at the station at seven in the morning, an hour before the train left, because I wanted to buy a coffee and read the newspaper. Tickets can be bought online, and I paid forty dollars for a seat in second class. First class costs about sixty dollars, but the only real difference is a little more space and a free snack. My seat was next to the window, and I could watch the villages, the cotton fields and the desert go past. A young man named Bobur sat beside me, and we talked for most of the trip. He is a student of history, and he was going to Bukhara to visit his grandmother.

Of course, train travel has some disadvantages too. In the summer the stations can be very hot and crowded, and tickets often sell out several days before a holiday. If you want to travel on a Friday or a Sunday, you should book at least a week in advance. Also, the luggage space is small, so please do not bring three suitcases. One medium bag is enough for a short trip.

Why do I prefer the train to the plane? First, you do not need to go through long security checks. Second, the stations are in the centre of the city, so you save time and money on taxis. Third, and most important for me, you see the country with your own eyes. At the end of the show I would like to hear from you. Send me a message about your favourite train journey, and I will read the best stories next Thursday. Now, let us listen to some music before our next guest arrives, a professor who will explain how the railway changed Central Asia.

intro: Har bir savol uchun 🔊 tugmasini bosib matnni tinglang (kerak bo'lsa qayta tinglang), so'ng javob bering.

items.prompt: How long has Gulnora worked as a guide?
items.audio:
Today the reporter Sanjar is interviewing Gulnora, a tour guide who has worked in the old city of Khiva for twelve years. Sanjar begins by asking why she chose this job. Gulnora smiles and says that she grew up inside the old walls, and as a child she used to follow the groups of tourists and listen to the stories. By the age of sixteen she knew every street, and she decided to study languages at university so that she could share her city with the world.

Sanjar then asks about a typical day. Gulnora explains that she meets her group at eight o'clock at the West Gate, because the morning light is best for photographs and the heat is not yet strong. The walk takes about four hours and includes the Kalta Minor minaret, the Juma Mosque with its forest of wooden columns, and the Tosh Hovli Palace. After the tour she takes everyone to a small family restaurant for a lunch of lamb soup and fresh bread.

The reporter wants to know about the most difficult part of her work. Gulnora says it is the summer weather. Temperatures can reach forty-five degrees, and some visitors forget to bring water or hats. She always carries extra bottles in her bag, and she tells her groups to rest in the shade at noon. Another challenge is the large number of tourists in April and October, when she sometimes leads thirty people at once. In that case she uses a small microphone so that everybody can hear her.

Next, Sanjar asks what advice she would give to a first-time visitor. Gulnora recommends staying for at least two nights, because Khiva looks completely different in the evening, when the walls turn orange and the streets become quiet. She also suggests wearing comfortable shoes, since the old stones are uneven. Finally, she says that visitors should talk to the local craftsmen, who make carpets, silk scarves and wooden boxes. She says that a small gift bought directly from a craftsman is the best memory of the trip. Sanjar thanks her for the interview and wishes her a busy and successful season.

items.prompt: How long was Jasur's flight?
items.audio:
When Jasur landed in London after a nine hour flight, he was tired but happy. He was going to spend two weeks there at a language school, and he had a big blue suitcase with all his clothes, books and a new winter coat. He waited at the baggage belt for almost forty minutes, watching the same bags go round and round. One by one, the other passengers took their luggage and left, and finally the belt stopped. His suitcase had not arrived.

Jasur felt worried, but he remembered his teacher's advice to stay calm and speak to the airline staff. He walked to the lost luggage office, where a woman called Mrs Taylor was sitting behind a desk. She asked him to fill in a form with his name, flight number and a description of the case. Jasur wrote that it was blue, medium sized, with a red ribbon on the handle. Mrs Taylor typed the information into her computer and discovered that the suitcase had been sent by mistake to Frankfurt, in Germany.

She told him not to worry, because the case would arrive in London the next morning on the first flight, and the airline would deliver it to his address by lunchtime. Jasur was relieved, but he asked what he should do tonight, because he had no clothes, no toothbrush and no phone charger. Mrs Taylor gave him a small emergency bag with a T-shirt, a toothbrush, soap and a towel. She also explained that the airline would pay up to eighty pounds for any necessary things he had to buy, if he kept the receipts.

Jasur took the underground to his host family's house, which was in a quiet street in the north of the city. The host mother, Mrs Evans, welcomed him with a cup of tea and lent him some pyjamas that belonged to her son. The next day the suitcase really did arrive at one o'clock, just as promised, and Jasur was delighted to see his winter coat again. He learned an important lesson from the adventure. From now on, he said, he would always keep a spare shirt, a charger and his medicine in his hand luggage, and he would take a photograph of his suitcase before every trip. He also told his friends to put a bright ribbon on their bags, because it makes them easier to recognise.

items.prompt: Who did Rachel travel with?
items.audio:
Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to my talk at the Adventure Club. My name is Rachel, and tonight I will tell you about the cycling holiday that I took last summer with my brother Tom through the north of Wales. We covered three hundred kilometres in eight days, and it was the best trip of my life, although it was also the hardest.

We started in the small town of Conwy, where we hired two mountain bikes for sixty pounds each for the whole week. The man at the shop gave us a map, a repair kit and a piece of good advice: always check the weather before leaving in the morning. We ignored him on the second day, and that was a mistake. Halfway up a long hill, heavy rain began, and within ten minutes we were wet to the skin. We found shelter in a tiny cafe, where the owner, an old lady called Gwen, made us hot chocolate and dried our jackets next to the fire.

The most beautiful part of the journey was the road around Snowdonia National Park. On the fourth day we cycled beside a blue lake called Llyn Padarn, and we stopped for lunch under a tree. Tom had a puncture there, and we spent an hour repairing the tyre, laughing at how little we knew about bicycles. Each evening we stayed in a different guesthouse. The cheapest was thirty pounds a night, with a big Welsh breakfast, and the most expensive was fifty, with a swimming pool.

There were difficult moments, too. On the sixth day Tom's knee started to hurt, and we had to take a train for part of the route. Still, we both agree that the trip taught us patience and teamwork. If you are thinking about a similar holiday, I have three tips. First, do not carry too much luggage; one small backpack is plenty. Second, drink water regularly, even when you do not feel thirsty. Third, start early in the day, because the afternoon wind can be strong. Now, I will show some photographs, and then I will be happy to answer your questions.

items.prompt: Why are the buses leaving later than usual?
items.audio:
Attention please, all passengers at the Central Bus Station. We have some important changes to the timetable this week, so please listen carefully. Because the road between Tashkent and Fergana is being repaired near the Kamchik Pass, all buses to Fergana, Andijan and Namangan will leave forty minutes later than usual until the end of the month.

The morning bus to Fergana, which normally leaves at seven fifteen, will now depart at five to eight from platform six. The afternoon bus will leave at two o'clock from platform seven. The journey, which usually takes five hours, may take up to six and a half, so passengers should bring food and water. The driver will make a stop at a roadside restaurant after three hours, and the break will last twenty minutes.

Tickets are available at the counters on the ground floor, in the mobile app and at the machines near the main entrance. A single ticket to Fergana costs seventy thousand soums, and a return ticket costs one hundred and twenty thousand. Students and pensioners get a discount of twenty percent if they show their cards. Please remember that tickets bought on the bus are more expensive, and the driver cannot accept cards, only cash.

We also have news about the services to Samarkand. A new express bus has started on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays. It has air conditioning, free wifi and large seats, and it goes without a stop in the middle. It leaves at nine in the morning and arrives at about two in the afternoon. The station manager, Mr Rustamov, says that many passengers asked for such a service. For safety, we remind everybody to keep their bags with them and not to leave them unattended in the waiting hall. Lost items can be collected at the information desk which is open every day until eight in the evening. The toilets are on the first floor, and the pharmacy is beside the cafe. Thank you for travelling with us, and we apologise for any delay.

items.prompt: How far are the Chimgan mountains from Tashkent?
items.audio:
Last weekend my friends and I went camping in the Chimgan mountains, about eighty kilometres from Tashkent. There were five of us: me, my cousin Farrukh, our classmates Madina and Otabek, and Madina's little brother Ali, who is only ten. We met at six in the morning at the bus stop, each of us carrying a heavy backpack with a tent, a sleeping bag, food for two days and warm clothes.

The minibus took us to the village at the bottom of the mountain in two hours, and we started walking at half past eight. The path was steep and stony, and after an hour Ali was already complaining that his legs hurt. Otabek, who is the most experienced of us, carried Ali's bag for a while, and we stopped every thirty minutes to drink water and eat dried apricots. At last, around one o'clock, we reached a flat green place beside a small river. It was perfect for the camp.

We put up the tents first, which took us almost an hour because Farrukh had forgotten the instructions. Then we collected wood and made a fire. Madina cooked rice with carrots and beef in a big pot, and it tasted wonderful after the long walk. In the evening, the temperature dropped to five degrees, and we sat around the fire in our jackets, singing songs and telling stories. Otabek played the guitar. Later, when we looked up, the sky was full of stars, more than any of us had ever seen in the city.

The next morning we woke up early because of the cold. We had tea and bread for breakfast and decided to climb to a small waterfall that a shepherd had told us about. It took forty minutes, and the view was worth it. Before going home, we cleaned the place carefully and took all our rubbish back with us, because we want the mountains to stay beautiful. The way back was easier since it was downhill. We reached Tashkent at eight in the evening, tired, dirty and very happy. Everyone agreed to repeat the trip in autumn, and this time Ali wants to bring his own small tent.

items.prompt: How long was the cruise?
items.audio:
This is Holiday Hour, and today our guest is Mr Peter Collins, who has just returned from a ten day cruise around the Mediterranean with his wife Susan. Peter, welcome to the programme. He begins by explaining that he never wanted to go on a cruise because he thought it would be boring and full of old people. His wife booked the holiday as a surprise for their fortieth wedding anniversary, and he did not want to disappoint her.

The ship left from Barcelona on a Saturday afternoon, and it carried about two thousand passengers. Peter was surprised by its size. It had five restaurants, three swimming pools, a cinema and even a small theatre. Their cabin was on the sixth deck, and it had a little balcony with a view of the sea. He says that the first night he did not sleep well because the waves moved the ship, but by the second day he was used to it.

The ship visited five ports: Marseille, Genoa, Rome, Naples and Valletta. In each port the passengers could go on an organised tour or explore by themselves. In Rome, Peter and Susan chose a guided tour of the Colosseum, which cost seventy euros each, and he thought it was excellent. In Naples they tried real Italian pizza in a tiny family restaurant, and he says it was the best meal of the whole trip. However, the days in port were short, and sometimes they had only six hours before they had to return to the ship.

The host asks about the disadvantages. Peter admits that cruises can be expensive, because drinks, trips and internet are not included in the price. The holiday cost them about three thousand euros in total. Another problem is the crowd; at breakfast there were long queues for the coffee machines. Still, Peter now says that he would go again, and he especially recommends it to people who hate packing and unpacking, because you carry your hotel with you. He advises listeners to book at least six months in advance to get a cheaper price, and to choose a cabin in the middle of the ship, where the movement is smaller. The host thanks him and promises to ask next week's guest about walking holidays in Scotland.

He begins by explaining that he never wanted to go on a cruise because he thought it would be boring and full of old people. His wife booked the holiday as a surprise for their fortieth wedding anniversary, and he did not want to disappoint her.

The ship left from Barcelona on a Saturday afternoon, and it carried about two thousand passengers. Peter was surprised by its size. It had five restaurants, three swimming pools, a cinema and even a small theatre. Their cabin was on the sixth deck, and it had a little balcony with a view of the sea. He says that the first night he did not sleep well because the waves moved the ship, but by the second day he was used to it.

The ship visited five ports: Marseille, Genoa, Rome, Naples and Valletta. In each port the passengers could go on an organised tour or explore by themselves. In Rome, Peter and Susan chose a guided tour of the Colosseum, which cost seventy euros each, and he thought it was excellent. In Naples they tried real Italian pizza in a tiny family restaurant, and he says it was the best meal of the whole trip. However, the days in port were short, and sometimes they had only six hours before they had to return to the ship.

The host asks about the disadvantages. Peter admits that cruises can be expensive, because drinks, trips and internet are not included in the price. The holiday cost them about three thousand euros in total. Another problem is the crowd; at breakfast there were long queues for the coffee machines. Still, Peter now says that he would go again, and he especially recommends it to people who hate packing and unpacking, because you carry your hotel with you. He advises listeners to book at least six months in advance to get a cheaper price, and to choose a cabin in the middle of the ship, where the movement is smaller. The host thanks him and promises to ask next week's guest about walking holidays in Scotland.

items.prompt: What is the name of the rental company?
items.audio:
Lola and her husband Anvar were planning a road trip around Georgia, and they decided to rent a car for a week. On Tuesday morning Lola called a rental company in Tbilisi called Caucasus Cars. A young woman named Nino answered and asked what kind of car they wanted. Lola said that they needed a small, economical car for two adults and two suitcases, because they did not want to spend too much on petrol.

Nino recommended a white Toyota hatchback. It cost thirty-five dollars a day, and the price included insurance and unlimited kilometres. A bigger car, such as a jeep, was fifty-five dollars a day, but Lola said that they did not need it. Nino also asked whether they had international driving licences. Lola replied that Anvar had one, and he would be the only driver. Nino said that this was fine, but a second driver could be added for five dollars a day.

Next, Lola asked about the pick up. Nino explained that the office was in the city centre, next to the central railway station, and it opened at nine o'clock. The car would be ready on Saturday morning, and the customers had to bring their passports, licences and a credit card for a deposit of two hundred dollars. The deposit would be returned a few days after they brought the car back, as long as there was no damage. She also advised them to take photographs of the car before driving away, to avoid any problems later.

Lola wanted to know about fuel. Nino said that the car would have a full tank at the start, and they should return it full as well, otherwise they would pay a fee. She added that petrol stations are easy to find on the main roads, but in the mountains they are rare, so it is wise to fill up whenever the tank is half empty. Lola also asked if the car had a navigation system. Nino answered that it did not, but she could give them a free paper map or they could use their phones. Lola agreed to book the car, paid a small advance by card and received a confirmation by email. She hung up and told Anvar that everything was ready. He was so pleased that he immediately started to plan the route to the mountain town of Kazbegi.

items.prompt: What is the name of the travel agency?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, everybody, and welcome to our travel evening at Sunrise Holidays. I am Kamola, a travel agent, and tonight I would like to talk about one of our most popular city breaks: four days in Prague, the capital of the Czech Republic. Many of our customers say that it is like a fairy tale city, with old bridges, colourful houses and a huge castle above the river.

Let us begin with the practical side. Our package includes return flights from Tashkent with a change in Istanbul, three nights in a three star hotel in the old town, and breakfast every morning. The price is six hundred and fifty dollars per person, if two people share a room. If you want a single room, you should add one hundred dollars. The flights leave on Thursday evenings, and you return on Monday afternoon, so you only miss two working days.

What should you do in Prague? On the first day, we suggest a walk across Charles Bridge early in the morning, before the crowds arrive. Then visit the castle, where you can see the cathedral and the beautiful gardens. Tickets cost about twenty dollars, and it is better to buy them online. The second day could be spent in the museums or on a river cruise, which lasts one hour and includes a cold drink. In the evening, do not miss a traditional dinner with roast pork, dumplings and local beer. If you do not drink alcohol, try the hot apple juice, which is very popular in winter.

Now a few tips. The best time to travel is April or September, when the weather is mild and the hotels are cheaper. In July and August the city is very busy, and in December it can be extremely cold. The local currency is the crown, not the euro, so we recommend that you change a small amount of money at the airport and then use your card. Public transport is excellent, and a three day ticket costs only about thirteen dollars. Finally, learn two or three words in Czech, such as thank you, because local people are always happy when visitors try to speak their language. If you have any questions, please come to my desk after the talk, and I will give each of you a free brochure.

items.prompt: How long has Captain Nilsson been a captain?
items.audio:
In this week's programme, journalist Dildora talks to Captain Nilsson, who has driven passenger ferries between Sweden and Finland for twenty-six years. She starts by asking him how he became a captain. He explains that his father was a fisherman, and as a boy he spent every summer on small boats in the harbour. At eighteen, he went to a maritime school in Gothenburg, where he studied for four years, and his first job was as an assistant on a cargo ship.

Dildora asks about his present ferry. It is a big white ship with eight decks, and it can carry sixteen hundred passengers and four hundred cars. The crossing takes about eleven hours overnight, leaving Stockholm at five in the afternoon and arriving in Helsinki at four in the morning. Many passengers sleep in comfortable cabins, while others enjoy the restaurants, the shops or the dance floor. Captain Nilsson says that, in his opinion, the sunset over the islands is the most beautiful moment of the trip.

What is the most difficult part of the job? The captain answers that it is the weather, especially in winter when ice forms in the sea and storms are common. Once, five years ago, a storm was so strong that the waves reached the fourth deck and the ferry arrived six hours late. He had to stay on the bridge for twenty hours without sleeping. However, he adds that safety is always the first priority. Before every trip, the crew checks the engines, the radios and the life boats, and every passenger watches a short safety video.

Finally, Dildora asks what he does in his free time. Captain Nilsson laughs and says that, surprisingly, he loves the water so much that he spends his holidays sailing in a small boat with his wife and their two daughters. He also grows tomatoes and potatoes in his garden. When he retires in four years, he wants to travel by train across Asia, because he has never seen the mountains. Dildora thanks him for the interesting conversation and wishes him calm seas and good weather. Next week she will talk to an air traffic controller about the work behind the busy skies. Do not miss it.

items.prompt: What is the manager's name?
items.audio:
Welcome to Green Door Hostel, everybody. My name is Sam, and I am the manager. Before you go to your rooms, I would like to explain a few things that will make your stay easier and more enjoyable. We have forty beds in total in six rooms, and each guest has a locker under the bed, so please bring a lock. If you forgot one, you can buy a small lock at reception for two euros.

Check in is from two in the afternoon, and check out is at eleven in the morning. If you need to leave later, you can keep your bags in the storage room for free. Breakfast is served from seven thirty to ten in the dining room, and it is included in the price, which is eighteen euros per night. It includes bread, jam, eggs, fruit and coffee. For dinner, you can use the shared kitchen on the ground floor, but please wash your plates afterwards, and do not leave food in the fridge for more than three days.

The wifi is free, and the password is written on the board behind reception. We have a quiet rule after ten at night, so if you want to talk or play music, please go to the common room or the garden. The front door is locked at midnight, but you will receive a key card if you plan to return late. Please do not lose it, because a new one costs ten euros. We also organise activities. Every Wednesday evening there is a free walking tour of the old town, which starts at six, and on Fridays we cook a big international dinner together.

Now some advice about the city. The nearest metro station is five minutes on foot, and a day ticket costs six euros. The best market is on Saturday mornings near the river, and it is cheap and full of local food. Be careful with your phone and wallet in crowded places, because pickpockets are active in tourist areas. If you have any problems, you can always find me or my colleague Elena at the desk. We are here day and night. Finally, please remember to turn off the lights and the air conditioning when you leave the room. We care about the environment, and we hope you do, too. Enjoy your stay, and thank you for choosing our hostel.

items.prompt: How old is Bekzod's grandfather?
items.audio:
Last winter I took a night train from Tashkent to Termez with my grandfather, and it was an experience that I will never forget. I am Bekzod, and I am nineteen years old. My grandfather, Abdulla, is seventy-eight, and he wanted to visit his old friend in the south before the winter got too cold. My parents were worried about his health, so I volunteered to travel with him.

The train left at nine in the evening from the main station, and we had a small compartment with four beds. Our travelling companions were a quiet teacher from Surkhandarya, named Shahlo, and her daughter, who was about six. Grandfather quickly started a conversation with them, and soon we were all drinking tea from the conductor's big kettle. The tea cost only a few thousand soums per glass, and it came with sugar and a little biscuit. The rhythm of the wheels made me feel sleepy, and I went to bed at eleven.

The journey lasted about thirteen hours, and in the middle of the night something unexpected happened. The train stopped for nearly an hour at a small station because of snow on the line. The conductor, a tall man with a moustache, explained that workers were clearing the rails and told us not to worry. Grandfather said that when he was young such stops were normal, and he began telling stories about his first train trip in nineteen sixty-two. He had gone to a technical college in Tashkent, and the journey took two days then.

When I woke up in the morning, the landscape outside had completely changed. There was no snow anymore, only dry hills and the sun shining on a wide river. We arrived in Termez at ten, almost two hours late. Grandfather's friend, Murod, was waiting on the platform with a bunch of flowers and a huge smile, and the two old men hugged each other for a long time. Watching them, I understood why my grandfather had wanted to make this trip so much. I stayed in Termez for three days, ate delicious melons even in winter, visited the ancient Buddhist ruins and took a plane back to Tashkent, because Grandfather decided to stay a month. Next time, I promise, I will take the train again.

items.prompt: In which month did they travel?
items.audio:
Hello, listeners. This week on our travel podcast I want to share my experience of a safari holiday in Kenya, which my husband Timur and I took in August. We had dreamed about it for years, and finally we saved enough money. The trip lasted nine days, and the main part took place in the Masai Mara reserve, which is about two hundred and fifty kilometres west of Nairobi.

We flew from Tashkent to Nairobi with one change in Dubai. The total flight took around twelve hours. In Nairobi, a driver called Joseph met us at the airport, and he was our guide for the whole safari. He was a cheerful man in his forties who knew everything about animals. The next day we travelled to the reserve in a white jeep with an open roof, and the road was so bumpy that I thought my back would break. After six hours, however, we arrived at our camp, which was a group of large tents with real beds and a hot shower.

The first morning, we got up at five thirty, before the sun rose, because that is the best time to see animals. We drank hot coffee and drove into the grassland. Within half an hour we saw a family of elephants with a tiny baby, and then a group of giraffes eating leaves from the tall trees. The most exciting moment came on the third day, when we found a lion sleeping under a bush only ten metres from our jeep. Joseph switched off the engine, and we sat in complete silence for twenty minutes. I could hear my own heart.

Of course, there were some difficulties. It was colder than we expected in the early mornings, so I advise taking a warm jacket. There was also a lot of dust, and my camera nearly stopped working. We had to follow strict rules: never leave the jeep, never feed the animals and never make loud noises. But these rules protect both tourists and wildlife. The whole trip cost four thousand dollars for two people, which is not cheap, but we think that every dollar was worth it. If you are planning a safari, the best months are July to October, when the animals gather near the rivers. Thank you for listening, and join me next week when I will talk about a winter holiday in Norway.

Hello, listeners. This week on our travel podcast I want to share my experience of a safari holiday in Kenya, which my husband Timur and I took in August. We had dreamed about it for years, and finally we saved enough money. The trip lasted nine days, and the main part took place in the Masai Mara reserve, which is about two hundred and fifty kilometres west of Nairobi.

We flew from Tashkent to Nairobi with one change in Dubai. The total flight took around twelve hours. In Nairobi, a driver called Joseph met us at the airport, and he was our guide for the whole safari. He was a cheerful man in his forties who knew everything about animals. The next day we travelled to the reserve in a white jeep with an open roof, and the road was so bumpy that I thought my back would break. After six hours, however, we arrived at our camp, which was a group of large tents with real beds and a hot shower.

The first morning, we got up at five thirty, before the sun rose, because that is the best time to see animals. We drank hot coffee and drove into the grassland. Within half an hour we saw a family of elephants with a tiny baby, and then a group of giraffes eating leaves from the tall trees. The most exciting moment came on the third day, when we found a lion sleeping under a bush only ten metres from our jeep. Joseph switched off the engine, and we sat in complete silence for twenty minutes. I could hear my own heart.

Of course, there were some difficulties. It was colder than we expected in the early mornings, so I advise taking a warm jacket. There was also a lot of dust, and my camera nearly stopped working. We had to follow strict rules: never leave the jeep, never feed the animals and never make loud noises. But these rules protect both tourists and wildlife. The whole trip cost four thousand dollars for two people, which is not cheap, but we think that every dollar was worth it. If you are planning a safari, the best months are July to October, when the animals gather near the rivers. Thank you for listening, and join me next week when I will talk about a winter holiday in Norway.

items.prompt: What job did Dilnoza apply for?
items.audio:
Good morning, listeners, and welcome to Career Corner. Today I want to tell you about a young woman named Dilnoza, who attended a job interview last week at a logistics company in Samarkand. She was applying for the position of assistant manager in the warehouse department, and she was very nervous because it was her first interview in three years.

Dilnoza arrived at the office at half past nine, thirty minutes before the appointment. The receptionist, a friendly man called Rustam, offered her a glass of water and asked her to wait in a small room with a few magazines. At ten o'clock, the director, Mrs Patterson, came out and invited her into a bright meeting room on the second floor.

Mrs Patterson began by asking Dilnoza to describe her previous job. Dilnoza explained that she had worked for four years at a furniture factory, where she organised deliveries and trained new employees. Then the director asked about her greatest weakness. Dilnoza answered honestly that she sometimes spent too much time checking small details, but she added that she was learning to trust her team more. Mrs Patterson smiled and said that honesty was exactly what the company wanted.

Next, the director explained the job. The assistant manager would lead a team of twelve workers, start every day at seven in the morning, and finish at four in the afternoon. The salary would be two thousand dollars a month, with a bonus every December if the warehouse met its targets. There was also a small canteen where employees could buy lunch at half price.

Towards the end, Dilnoza asked about training. Mrs Patterson replied that all new managers attended a two week course in Tashkent, paid for by the company. Finally, she said she would phone every candidate by Friday evening.

On Thursday afternoon, Dilnoza received a call. She had been chosen from nine candidates! She will start on the first Monday of next month. Her advice for anyone attending an interview is simple: arrive early, be honest, and prepare some questions of your own. Thank you for listening, and join us again next week for more career tips.

items.prompt: How long did Aziz work in a hotel?
items.audio:
Welcome back to Small Business Hour. This week I spoke with Aziz Karimov, who opened his own bakery six months ago in the centre of Namangan. I asked him how the idea began, and he told me a very honest story.

Aziz explained that for ten years he worked as a baker for a large hotel. He enjoyed the job, but he always dreamed of having a place of his own. Three years ago he started saving money, putting away two hundred dollars every month. When he had saved nearly six thousand dollars, his uncle Farhod offered to lend him another four thousand, and that made the dream possible.

Finding the right building was not easy. Aziz looked at eleven different shops before he chose a small one near a school and a bus stop. He said that the location was the most important decision, because hungry students pass by every morning at eight o'clock. The rent was four hundred dollars a month, which he thought was fair.

The first weeks were difficult. Aziz baked alone from three in the morning, and he often fell asleep on a chair in the afternoon. Only a few customers came, and he almost lost hope. Then his wife, Malika, suggested a free sample of warm bread for everybody who walked past. The idea worked wonderfully. Within one week, there was a queue outside the door every morning.

Today Aziz employs three people: two bakers and a young cashier named Zilola. The most popular product is a sweet cheese pastry, which sells out before noon. He also delivers cakes for weddings and birthdays, and this brings in nearly half of his profit.

I asked Aziz what advice he would give to future business owners. He thought for a moment and said that people should never borrow more than they can repay, and that they should always listen to their customers. His next plan is to open a second shop in Kokand next spring. We wish him good luck, and we will be back after the news.

items.prompt: How long has Nigora been helping employees?
items.audio:
Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to today's workshop on money at work. My name is Nigora Tursunova, and for fifteen years I have helped employees prepare for difficult conversations with their managers. Today we will talk about one of the most stressful of all: asking for a higher salary.

Let me begin with a short story. Last year, a client of mine named Bekzod worked as an accountant in a medium-sized company. He had been in the same job for four years and had never asked for more money. When he finally compared his salary with similar jobs, he discovered that he earned almost twenty percent less than other accountants in the city. He came to me feeling angry, but I told him that anger is a poor adviser.

We started by collecting facts. First, we found salary information on job websites and in a report published by the chamber of commerce. Second, we made a list of his achievements. For example, he had reduced the cost of paper and printing by a third, and he had trained two new colleagues without extra pay. I always say that managers listen to results, not to complaints.

Then we chose the right moment. Many people ask at a bad time, such as on a Friday afternoon, when everybody is tired. Bekzod waited until the company finished its yearly report, because that was when the director was most pleased. He asked for a meeting on a Tuesday morning and began the conversation politely, by thanking the director for her support.

He did not ask for a small increase. He named a clear figure, and it was a little higher than he really wanted, which left space to negotiate. The director thought about it for a week. In the end she offered him fifteen percent more and an extra five days of holiday. Bekzod accepted immediately.

So remember three rules: prepare your facts, choose your moment, and ask for a specific amount. Now let us take a short break, and afterwards you can practise in pairs.

items.audio:
Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to today's workshop on money at work. My name is Nigora Tursunova, and for fifteen years I have helped employees prepare for difficult conversations with their managers. Today we will talk about one of the most stressful of all: asking for a higher salary.

Let me begin with a short story. Last year, a client of mine named Bekzod worked as an accountant in a medium-sized company. He had been in the same job for four years and had never asked for more money. When he finally compared his salary with similar jobs, he discovered that he earned almost twenty percent less than other accountants in the city. He came to me feeling angry, but I told him that anger is a poor adviser.

We started by collecting facts. First, we found salary information on job websites and in a report published by the chamber of commerce. Second, we made a list of his achievements. For example, he had reduced the cost of paper and printing by a third, and he had trained two new colleagues without extra pay. I always say that managers listen to results, not to complaints.

Then we chose the right moment. Many people ask at a bad time, such as on a Friday afternoon, when everybody is tired. Bekzod waited until the company finished its yearly report, because that was when the director was most pleased. He asked for a meeting on a Tuesday morning and began the conversation politely, by thanking the director for her support.

He did not ask for a small increase. He named a clear figure, and it was a little higher than he really wanted, which left space to negotiate. The director thought about it for a week. In the end she offered him fifteen percent more and an extra five days of holiday. Bekzod accepted immediately.

items.prompt: What is Laura's profession?
items.audio:
In this week's episode of our podcast about modern work, I want to share the experience of a woman called Laura Bennett, who has worked from home for two years. Laura is a translator, and before the change she travelled ninety minutes every day to an office in the middle of London.

Laura says the biggest advantage was time. She used to leave the house at seven and return at half past seven in the evening. Now she wakes at eight, walks her dog in the park, and starts work at nine. She calculated that she saves almost three hours every day, and that she also saves about a hundred and fifty pounds a month on train tickets.

However, working from home was not easy at first. Her flat is small, and she began working on the sofa. After a few weeks her back hurt, and she felt tired all the time. A friend advised her to create a proper workplace, so she bought a desk and a comfortable chair, and she put them in the quietest corner of the bedroom. She also decided to close the laptop every evening at six o'clock. Without this rule, she said, work slowly takes over your whole life.

Another problem was loneliness. In the office she had chatted with colleagues at lunch, and at home she sometimes went a whole day without speaking to anyone. To solve this, Laura joined a co-working space once a week, where she meets other freelancers and enjoys a coffee with them. She also phones her sister every Wednesday.

I asked her whether she would return to an office. She laughed and said that she might, but only for two days a week. She believes the perfect job mixes both worlds. Companies, she thinks, should trust their employees more, because people who feel trusted usually work harder.

That is all for today. Next week we will visit a company in Leeds that has introduced a four day working week. Until then, take care of yourselves.

items.prompt: What is Madina's job?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, and welcome to the customer information line of Silk Road Bank. I am going to tell you about our new savings account for young adults, which has been very popular since we launched it in January.

To begin with, let me describe a typical customer. Her name is Madina, she is twenty three years old, and she works as a nurse at a city hospital. Last month she visited our branch on Navoi Street because she wanted to start saving for a small flat. She spoke to an adviser called Mr Ismoilov, who explained the main features of the account.

First, the account pays interest of seven percent a year, which is higher than most ordinary accounts. The interest is added every three months, so the money grows steadily. Second, there is no monthly fee, and customers can open the account with only fifty dollars. Third, savers may take out their money at any time, but if they withdraw more than twice in a year, the interest for that year becomes lower.

Mr Ismoilov also suggested a clever habit. He advised Madina to set up an automatic transfer on the day she receives her salary, which for her is the fifth of every month. In this way, she saves before she has the chance to spend. Madina decided to transfer one hundred and twenty dollars each month. In five years, she will have saved more than eight thousand dollars, including interest, and that will be enough for a deposit on a flat.

What do you need to open the account? Bring your passport and a document that shows where you work. If you are under eighteen, a parent must come with you. The whole process takes about twenty minutes.

We also have a mobile application, so you can check your balance anytime. If you ever lose your bank card, please call our emergency number immediately, and we will block it within minutes.

Thank you for calling Silk Road Bank. If you would like to speak to an adviser, please stay on the line, and we will connect you shortly.

items.prompt: What does Gulnora sell?
items.audio:
Today's report from our radio series about local business takes us to the Chorsu bazaar, where we meet Gulnora Yusupova. Gulnora is fifty two years old, and for twenty years she has sold dried fruit and nuts from the same small stall near the entrance.

I visited her at six o'clock in the morning, when the market was just waking up. Gulnora was already arranging apricots, raisins and walnuts in neat piles. She told me that the day begins even earlier at her house. She wakes at four, drinks tea, and drives to the wholesale market to buy fresh goods before the best products disappear.

I asked her what makes a successful seller. She said that trust is everything. Her customers know that she never mixes old fruit with new, and that she always lets people taste before they buy. Many of them have come to her for ten years or more. One elderly man, Mr Anvar, visits every Saturday and buys exactly one kilogram of dried figs.

The work is hard, of course. Gulnora stands for ten hours, and in summer the heat under the roof is terrible. In winter her fingers become cold, and she wears woollen gloves with the ends cut off so she can count the money. Her profit changes during the year. The best season is just before the holidays, when customers buy large bags of nuts as presents. In those weeks she earns three times more than usual.

Recently her daughter Sevara suggested that Gulnora should sell online. At first Gulnora laughed, because she does not trust the internet. But she agreed to try. Sevara made a simple page with photographs, and in the first month eleven people ordered from outside the city. Gulnora is now proud and says she is never too old to learn.

When I left the bazaar, the morning crowd was arriving. Gulnora waved, smiled, and weighed a bag of raisins for her first customer of the day.

items.prompt: How long has Eastern Foods existed?
items.audio:
Good morning, everybody, and thank you for gathering in the main hall. I have an important announcement to make, and I want to tell you the news myself before you read it in the newspapers.

As you know, our company, Eastern Foods, has been producing biscuits and sweets for thirty years. Last night, after six months of private discussions, the board agreed to join with Golden Harvest, a larger company from Almaty. From the first of September, we will work together under a new name, which is Central Asia Foods.

I understand that many of you are worried, so let me answer the three questions I have heard most often. First, will anybody lose their job? The answer is no. Nobody will be dismissed because of this change. In fact, we expect to hire about eighty new workers during the next two years, because the combined company will sell to more countries. Second, will your salary change? Your pay will stay the same for at least twelve months, and after that, everybody will be offered the same conditions as employees in Almaty. Third, will the factory close? Absolutely not. The factory in Andijan will remain our main production centre, and we plan to build a new warehouse next to it.

There will, of course, be some changes. The head office will move to a bigger building in Tashkent, and some managers will travel to Almaty for training. We will also introduce new computer software for orders, and each department will receive a lesson on how to use it in the first week of October.

Why are we doing this? The market is becoming more difficult, and small producers find it hard to compete with big imported brands. Together, we will be able to buy ingredients at lower prices and invest in modern machines.

My door is always open, and my assistant, Mrs Rakhimova, will organise small meetings for those with questions. Thank you for your hard work, and thank you for your trust. I am confident that the best years of our company are still ahead of us.

items.prompt: How long was Timur a teacher?
items.audio:
Hello and welcome to Second Chances, the programme about people who start a new life at work. Today I am talking to Timur Saidov, who was a school teacher for fourteen years and is now a computer programmer. Timur, thank you for joining us.

Timur began by explaining why he left teaching. He said that he loved children, but he felt tired and underpaid. His salary was only four hundred dollars a month, and he had to give private lessons in the evening to support his family. One day his wife, Feruza, who works in a bank, told him that he was always at work and never at home. That conversation changed everything.

His first step was to choose a new field. He had always been good at mathematics, so he decided to try programming. He started with free videos on the internet, studying two hours every night after his children went to bed. After six months, he enrolled in an evening course at a technology academy, which cost nine hundred dollars. His brother Alisher lent him the money.

The hardest period came during the second year. Timur sent his documents to more than forty companies and received only three answers. He was almost thirty nine, and employers preferred younger candidates. He nearly gave up, but his teacher at the academy told him that his experience of explaining difficult ideas was valuable. In the end, a small software company in Tashkent offered him a junior position.

Today he earns eleven hundred dollars a month, and he works mostly from home. He says that the first year was stressful because he was the oldest person in the team and made many mistakes. Yet his colleagues were kind, and slowly he gained confidence.

I asked whether he regrets his decision. Timur smiled and said that he misses his students, so he now teaches a free programming club for teenagers on Saturdays. His advice to listeners is clear: it is never too late to change, but you need patience, a plan and support from the people you love.

items.prompt: How long has Kamila been a freelancer?
items.audio:
Welcome, everyone, to this evening's talk for young people who are thinking about working for themselves. I am Kamila Rahimova, and for six years I have been a freelance graphic designer. Tonight I would like to describe how my work really looks, because many people imagine it to be easier than it is.

I left my office job in the spring of two thousand and eighteen. At that time, I had only three clients and about two months of savings in my bank account. My father warned me that I was taking a big risk, and he was partly right. In the first year my income was very uneven. In March I earned almost two thousand dollars, but in April I earned less than three hundred.

The lesson I learned was to plan for the bad months. Today, I keep an emergency fund that covers six months of expenses, and I never spend all of the money from a good month. I also learned to ask for a deposit of thirty percent before I begin any project. Otherwise, some clients disappear after receiving the finished work, and that happened to me twice.

Another difficulty is organising time. Nobody tells a freelancer when to start or finish, so you must be your own manager. I work from nine until five, and I use a simple notebook to list three important tasks for each day. When I complete them, I stop, even if it is only three in the afternoon.

Finding customers is perhaps the biggest challenge. At first I used websites where designers compete for small jobs, but the pay was low. Now most of my clients find me through recommendations. One happy owner of a restaurant told her friends, and within two months I had four new projects.

Is it worth it? For me, absolutely. I decide which jobs to accept, I travel when I want, and I earn nearly twice my old salary. But it demands discipline and courage. If you are ready, start slowly, keep your job for a while, and build your first clients in the evenings. Thank you, and now I will gladly answer your questions.

items.prompt: Where did the accident happen last month?
items.audio:
Attention, please, all employees of the Bukhara Textile Factory. This is an important announcement from the safety department, and I ask you to listen carefully. Please also tell your colleagues if they are working in a different part of the building.

As you know, last month there was a small accident in the packing hall. A worker slipped on a wet floor and hurt his ankle. Fortunately, he is already recovering and will return next Monday. After an investigation, the management has decided to introduce new rules, which will begin on the first day of next month.

First, everybody who enters the production area must wear safety shoes with rubber soles. The company will give each employee one pair free of charge. If you need a larger size, please tell Mrs Davletova in the supply office by this Friday. Second, protective glasses are now required near the cutting machines. They are available in the blue boxes by the main door, and they must be returned at the end of each shift.

Third, we are going to paint yellow lines on the floor. These lines show the safe walking path, and no one should leave the path while machines are working. Please also report every spill immediately and never leave it for the next person. A clean floor is the cheapest way to prevent accidents.

Fourth, there will be a compulsory training session for all staff. It will take place in the canteen, and it will last ninety minutes. Employees from the morning shift will attend on Tuesday at two o'clock, and employees from the evening shift will attend on Wednesday at nine in the morning. The company will pay for the extra time. A doctor from the city hospital will also teach everybody basic first aid.

Finally, we are installing a new emergency alarm, and next Thursday we will test it. Do not be afraid when you hear a loud sound. Remember that the main exit is on the north side, and the meeting point is the car park.

Safety is everyone's responsibility. Thank you for your cooperation, and please keep working carefully.

items.prompt: What does Otabek grow?
items.audio:
This is the story of a telephone call that took place last Tuesday between Otabek Nazarov, a young farmer, and a loan officer at the regional agricultural bank. I would like to tell you what they discussed, because many listeners have asked how business loans actually work.

Otabek called at ten in the morning. He explained that he owns a small farm near Fergana where he grows tomatoes and cucumbers in greenhouses. He wants to build two more greenhouses, and the total cost will be about fourteen thousand dollars. He has saved four thousand dollars himself, so he needs to borrow the remaining ten thousand.

The officer, a calm woman named Mrs Hasanova, thanked him and asked several questions. First, she wanted to know how long the farm had been running. Otabek answered that it had operated for five years. Second, she asked about his income. He said that last year he earned about nineteen thousand dollars, after paying for seeds, water and workers. Third, she asked whether he had any other debts. He admitted that he still owed a small amount for a tractor, which he would finish repaying in eight months.

Then Mrs Hasanova explained the conditions. The bank could offer a loan for three years with an interest rate of eleven percent. Otabek would repay the money in monthly parts of about three hundred and thirty dollars. She also mentioned that, because he works in agriculture, he would not need to pay anything during the first three months, which would help him while the greenhouses were being built.

To apply, he would have to send several documents. These included a copy of his passport, proof of land ownership, a business plan and statements from his bank for the last year. Mrs Hasanova advised him to prepare the business plan carefully, with clear numbers about future sales.

Otabek thanked her warmly and promised to visit the branch on Thursday. After the call, he said he felt much calmer, because he now knew exactly what to prepare. A good conversation with the right person, he says, is worth more than a week of worry.

items.prompt: What does Sardor sell?
items.audio:
Hello, and welcome to the weekly business podcast for young entrepreneurs. My guest today is Sardor Ergashev, who runs an online shop that sells handmade leather bags. He is only twenty six, but his shop already sends parcels to eight countries. Sardor, tell us how it all started.

Sardor explained that the idea came from his grandfather, a shoemaker in Margilan, who taught him to work with leather when he was a boy. After university, Sardor worked in an insurance company, but he spent every evening making bags in the garage. His friends liked them so much that they began asking him to sell some. He put photographs on a social media page, and within a week he had sold six bags.

The real growth began when he made his own website. It cost him about three hundred dollars, and he built it with the help of a free course. He says that good photographs are the secret of selling online, because customers cannot touch the product. He bought a simple camera and learned to take pictures near a large window, where the light is soft.

He also talked about mistakes. In his first year, he promised delivery in three days, but the post office often needed ten. Customers became upset, and some wrote bad comments. Now he explains the real time clearly on the page, and he sends a message at each step of the journey. Complaints have fallen by almost ninety percent.

Currently Sardor employs two craftsmen and one assistant who answers messages. The average bag costs eighty dollars, and last month the shop earned around nine thousand dollars. After paying for materials, salaries and delivery, about a quarter remained as profit.

When I asked about his plans, he said that he wants to open a small workshop where tourists can watch the bags being made. He believes that people enjoy buying something when they know the story behind it. We wish him success, and we will return after a short break with advice about paying taxes.

After university, Sardor worked in an insurance company, but he spent every evening making bags in the garage. His friends liked them so much that they began asking him to sell some. He put photographs on a social media page, and within a week he had sold six bags.

The real growth began when he made his own website. It cost him about three hundred dollars, and he built it with the help of a free course. He says that good photographs are the secret of selling online, because customers cannot touch the product. He bought a simple camera and learned to take pictures near a large window, where the light is soft.

He also talked about mistakes. In his first year, he promised delivery in three days, but the post office often needed ten. Customers became upset, and some wrote bad comments. Now he explains the real time clearly on the page, and he sends a message at each step of the journey. Complaints have fallen by almost ninety percent.

Currently Sardor employs two craftsmen and one assistant who answers messages. The average bag costs eighty dollars, and last month the shop earned around nine thousand dollars. After paying for materials, salaries and delivery, about a quarter remained as profit.

When I asked about his plans, he said that he wants to open a small workshop where tourists can watch the bags being made. He believes that people enjoy buying something when they know the story behind it. We wish him success, and we will return after a short break with advice about paying taxes.

items.prompt: How long has Rustam worked as a financial adviser?
items.audio:
Good evening, and thank you for joining this free lecture, organised by the city library, on planning your retirement. My name is Rustam Aliyev, and I have worked as a financial adviser for twenty two years. Many people think that retirement is a topic for old people. In fact, the best time to think about it is when you are young.

Let me start with an example. Imagine two friends, Ilhom and Shirin. Ilhom began saving when he was twenty five. He put aside only fifty dollars each month. Shirin began at thirty five, but she saved one hundred dollars each month. When they both reach sixty five, who do you think has more money? Surprisingly, it is Ilhom. The reason is time. His money had ten extra years to grow, and small amounts become large when they stay in the account for a long time.

Now let me explain the three main sources of income in retirement. The first is the state pension, which is paid by the government. It is useful, but for most people it covers only about half of their normal expenses. The second is the pension from your employer, and I always advise people to check whether their company offers one. Some employers add money to your account if you also contribute. The third is your own savings, which you control completely.

What can you do today? First, make a simple budget and see how much you spend each month. Second, decide on a fixed amount, even if it is small, and move it to a separate account on payday. Third, avoid keeping all your money in one place. Some people prefer property, others prefer bank deposits, and a wise person uses both.

A final warning concerns inflation. Prices rise slowly over the years, so money hidden under a mattress loses value. Please do not trust any person who promises to double your money in one month, because that is almost always a trick.

Thank you for listening. There are leaflets on the table by the door, and I will stay for half an hour to answer questions.

items.prompt: Where is the new office?
items.audio:
Good morning, colleagues, and thank you for being on time. I would like to take a few minutes to talk about our move to the new office, which will take place at the end of this month. I know that many of you have questions, so I will try to answer the most important ones now.

First, the location. The new building is on Amir Temur Avenue, next to the metro station. For most of you, the journey will actually become shorter. The old office has been cramped for years, as everyone knows. The new one has three floors, and our company will occupy the second and the third. The ground floor contains a cafe and a small shop, where you will be able to buy lunch.

Second, the schedule. The movers will arrive on Friday the twenty sixth, at eight in the morning, and they will carry the furniture and the computers. Please put all your personal things into the boxes that Mrs Karimova will give you on Wednesday. Write your name and your department on each box in large letters. The office will be closed for the weekend, and everybody should come to the new address on Monday.

Third, the layout. We have decided to try an open space for the sales and marketing teams, because they talk to each other all day. However, the accountants will have a separate quiet room, as they need to concentrate on numbers. There will also be two small meeting rooms, which you can book on the computer, and a relaxation area with sofas and a table tennis table.

Fourth, parking. Unfortunately, the new building has only twenty places for cars, so we will use a lottery system. The metro and the buses are an excellent alternative, and the company will pay half of the cost of a monthly ticket.

Finally, I want to thank the whole team for your patience. Moving is stressful, but I truly believe that the new place will make our work happier and more efficient. If you have any concerns, please write to Mr Yusupov in the administration department. Now, let us return to work, and thank you again.

items.prompt: Where is Bobur from?
items.audio:
Hello, listeners. In today's programme we look at a way of starting a career without going to university: the apprenticeship. To illustrate, I will tell you about Bobur Hamidov, an eighteen year old from Karshi who recently began training as an electrician.

Bobur finished school last summer with average marks. His parents hoped that he would study economics, but he knew that it was not for him. He enjoyed practical work, and he often helped his uncle repair lamps and sockets at home. In September he saw an advertisement for an apprenticeship at a building company, and he decided to apply.

The selection was not simple. First, there was a written test about basic mathematics, and sixty people took it. Then twenty were invited to an interview, and in the end only eight were accepted. Bobur says that the director asked him a strange question: what would he do if a colleague made a dangerous mistake? He answered that he would speak to the colleague immediately and, if necessary, inform the supervisor. The director nodded and wrote something down.

The programme lasts three years. Four days a week, Bobur works on real building sites with an experienced electrician named Mr Sultanov, and one day a week he studies theory at a technical college. For this, he receives a monthly payment of two hundred and fifty dollars, which will increase each year. When he finishes, he will earn at least ten times more than his first payment, though this depends on his skills.

Bobur says that the first week was frightening. He carried heavy cables up five floors and made a mistake with a switch. Mr Sultanov did not shout. He simply showed him again, patiently, and said that everyone starts this way. Now Bobur can read building plans and install lights without any help.

Experts say that skilled workers like electricians will be needed for many years, because every new building requires them. Bobur's advice for school leavers is to look at all the options. A university is not the only road, and a good trade can bring both security and pride.

items.audio:
Good evening, listeners, and welcome to Active Life. Tonight our guest is Dilnoza Karimova, a teacher from Samarkand who ran her first marathon last spring. Dilnoza says she never imagined herself as a runner. Three years ago she could hardly run for five minutes without stopping, because she spent most of her days sitting in a classroom or at her desk marking homework.

The change began when her younger brother Jasur challenged her to join a charity race of five kilometres. She finished it in thirty-eight minutes and felt proud, but also very tired. That evening she decided to follow a proper training plan. She chose a programme that lasted twenty weeks and asked her to run four days a week. Three of those runs were short or medium, and the fourth was a long run on Sunday morning, which grew a little longer every week.

Dilnoza admits that the hardest part was not her legs but her motivation. In the dark winter mornings she often wanted to stay in bed. To solve this problem she found a running partner, a neighbour called Mark, who is originally from Manchester. They agreed to meet at six thirty outside her building, and because Mark was waiting for her in the cold, she never dared to cancel.

Food was another important lesson. At first she ate almost nothing before a long run and felt weak after twelve kilometres. A sports nutritionist told her to eat porridge with honey and a banana two hours before running, and to carry a small bag of dried apricots. After that change her energy improved immediately.

On the day of the marathon the weather was warm, and she started slowly on purpose. Many runners rushed ahead, but she kept a steady speed and passed several of them later. Around the thirty-second kilometre she hit what runners call the wall, and her legs felt like stone. She repeated to herself that she only needed to reach the next water station. Finally she crossed the finish line in four hours and twenty minutes, with her whole family cheering.

Her advice for beginners is simple: start small, be patient, never skip rest days, and find someone to share the road with you.

items.prompt: Where is the talk taking place?
items.audio:
Hello everyone, and thank you for coming to this morning's talk at the community health centre. My name is Doctor Malika Rakhimova, and today I would like to speak about the most discussed meal of the day: breakfast.

Many people tell me they simply do not have time to eat in the morning. They drink a cup of coffee and run to the bus. I understand this completely, because I used to do exactly the same when I was a student. However, after a night without food, your body needs fuel. A good breakfast helps you concentrate, keeps your mood stable, and stops you from eating too many sweets before lunch.

So what makes a good breakfast? First, it should contain protein. Eggs, yoghurt, cottage cheese or a handful of nuts are all excellent choices. Protein keeps you feeling full for much longer than bread alone. Second, it should include slow carbohydrates, such as oats, whole grain bread or fruit. These give your brain a steady supply of energy through the morning. Third, try to add something fresh, like a tomato, a cucumber or an apple.

I must also warn you about some breakfast traps. Many cereals sold in colourful boxes contain a surprising amount of sugar. One bowl can have as much sugar as two chocolate biscuits. Fruit juice from a carton is another trap, because it has less fibre than a whole fruit. If you love juice, please drink only a small glass.

Here is a quick plan for busy people. On Sunday evening, boil six eggs and keep them in the fridge. Prepare a jar of oats with milk and let it stand overnight. In the morning you only need to add a spoonful of honey and some berries. It takes three minutes.

Finally, children are especially affected. A study in a school in Tashkent found that pupils who ate breakfast scored higher in morning tests than pupils who skipped it. So please make sure your children eat before school.

Now, before the break, I will answer your questions, and after that we will taste some healthy recipes together in the kitchen next door.

items.prompt: Why was Bobur's back painful?
items.audio:
Last Tuesday morning, Bobur Tursunov woke up with a terrible pain in his back. He had spent the whole weekend helping his cousin move to a new flat, carrying boxes and furniture up four floors, and now he could hardly stand straight. He decided to call the clinic near his home.

The receptionist, a friendly woman called Nargiza, answered on the third ring. Bobur explained that he needed to see a doctor as soon as possible. Nargiza asked him for his full name and his date of birth, and then she asked whether he had visited the clinic before. Bobur said that he had been there two years ago for a sore throat. She found his file on the computer and told him that his family doctor, Doctor Alimov, was away on holiday until the end of the week.

Bobur was disappointed, but Nargiza suggested another doctor, a young specialist named Doctor Yusupova, who had an appointment free that same afternoon at a quarter past three. She added that it would be better to arrive ten minutes early, because new patients had to fill in a short form. Bobur wrote down the time and thanked her.

Then Nargiza asked whether he was taking any medicine. Bobur said that he had taken one painkiller in the morning, and it had not helped much. She told him not to take any more until he had talked to the doctor, and she reminded him to bring his identity card and his insurance paper.

At the clinic that afternoon, Doctor Yusupova examined his back carefully and asked him to bend forward and then to the side. She explained that he had pulled a muscle and that nothing was seriously wrong. She advised him to rest for two days, to use a warm compress for twenty minutes in the evening, and to start gentle stretching exercises on Friday. She also gave him a cream to rub into the sore place twice a day.

Bobur left the clinic relieved. On the way home he promised himself that next time he would ask his cousin to hire movers.

items.prompt: When do the adult beginners' classes take place?
items.audio:
Attention please, all members and visitors of the Riverside Sports Centre. This is an important announcement about our new swimming programme, which begins next month.

After many requests from parents and local residents, we are happy to tell you that the main pool will now be open for lessons on weekday evenings. Beginners' classes for adults will take place on Monday and Wednesday from seven until eight in the evening. Our children's group, for pupils between six and ten years old, will meet on Tuesday and Thursday at five o'clock. Each lesson lasts forty-five minutes, and every group has no more than twelve people so that the coach can pay attention to everyone.

The lessons will be taught by Coach Sherzod Normatov, who was a national junior champion in backstroke and has worked with young swimmers for eleven years. He will be helped by two assistants, Laura from Spain and Aziza from Bukhara, both of whom are qualified lifeguards.

Please note several rules. First, everyone must take a shower before entering the water. Second, swimming caps are compulsory, and you can borrow one at the front desk for a small deposit. Third, children under eight must always be accompanied by an adult in the changing rooms. Finally, please do not run on the wet floor, because it is very slippery.

The price of a monthly course is two hundred thousand sum for adults and one hundred and fifty thousand for children. Members of the centre receive a discount of ten percent. If you bring a friend, you will both get an extra free lesson. You can register at the front desk, on our website, or by telephone between nine in the morning and six in the evening.

We also want to remind you that the small pool, which is warmer, is reserved for older people and for those who are recovering from injuries. It is open every morning except Sunday.

The first free trial lesson will be held on Saturday at ten o'clock, and everybody is welcome to come and try. Thank you for your attention, and we hope to see you in the water very soon.

items.prompt: What was Gulnora's job or status?
items.audio:
Welcome back to the programme. Our next guest is Gulnora Saidova, a university student who stopped eating meat two years ago. Gulnora, thank you for joining us.

Thank you for inviting me. Well, my story is not very dramatic. The presenter asks why she changed her diet, and Gulnora answers that it started with a school project about farms. She visited a large chicken farm with her classmates and felt uncomfortable about the conditions there. A few weeks later she decided to try a vegetarian month, just as an experiment, and she never went back.

The presenter then asks about her family, because in Uzbekistan meat is a very important part of many meals. Gulnora laughs and says that her grandmother was shocked. Her grandmother kept offering her soup with beef and said she would become weak. Gulnora's mother was more understanding, but she worried about her health, so the whole family went to see a doctor together. The doctor explained that a vegetarian diet can be perfectly healthy if you eat enough beans, lentils, nuts, eggs and dairy, and if you check your iron and vitamin levels once a year.

The presenter wonders whether it is difficult to eat out with friends. Gulnora says that it was hard at the beginning, because many cafes only offered salad. Now the situation is much better, and she even found a small restaurant near her university where the chef makes a wonderful pumpkin samsa and a lentil soup. She also likes to cook at home. Her favourite dish is stuffed peppers with rice, herbs and chickpeas.

About money, she says that vegetarian food is usually cheaper, especially in summer, when vegetables at the bazaar cost very little. She spends roughly a third less on food than before.

As a final question, the presenter asks what advice she would give. Gulnora replies that people should not feel pressure to change quickly. She suggests starting with one meat-free day a week, learning a few easy recipes, and being kind to friends and relatives who eat differently. Respect, she says, works better than arguing.
