items.prompt: How long has the professor studied sleep?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, students. Today I want to talk about something that most of you probably do not get enough of: sleep. My name is Professor Anvar Ismoilov, and I have studied sleep for almost twenty years.

Let me begin with a simple fact. Teenagers and young adults need between eight and ten hours of sleep each night. Yet in a survey at our university last year, the average student slept only six hours. That is a serious gap, and it has consequences.

When you sleep, your brain is not resting in the way people often imagine. In fact, it is very busy. During deep sleep it organises the information you learned during the day and moves it into long-term memory. This is why studying all night before an exam is a bad idea. You may read more pages, but you will remember less of them.

items.prompt: How many teams take part?
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Spring Youth Football Tournament in Namangan. My name is Rustam Aliyev, and I am the chief organiser of today's event. Before the first match starts, I would like to explain the schedule and a few important rules.

This year we have sixteen teams from six different cities, and more than two hundred young players between twelve and fifteen years old. The tournament will last two days. Today we will play the group matches on four pitches, and tomorrow we will have the quarter-finals, the semi-finals and the final. The final will start at four o'clock tomorrow afternoon on the main pitch, which has real grass and a small stand for the supporters.

Every match consists of two halves of twenty minutes, with a break of five minutes in the middle. If a group match ends in a draw, each team gets one point. A win brings three points. In the knockout games, if the score is level after the second half, we will go straight to penalties.

I want to thank our sponsors, a local bakery and a sports shop, who have given us the medals, the trophies and the water for the players. The winners will receive a silver cup and a ball signed by a famous goalkeeper, who will also be visiting us tomorrow to meet the children.

Please remember some practical points. Players must wear shin guards, and no metal studs are allowed on the boots. Parents are asked to stay behind the white line along the pitch and to support all the teams politely. The referees are volunteers, many of them former players, and their decisions are final. A doctor and two nurses are on duty in the white tent next to the car park, in case someone is hurt.

There is a small cafe near the entrance, where you can buy tea, sandwiches and fruit. Please use the rubbish bins, because we want to leave this field as clean as we found it.

Above all, remember that football is a game, and the most important thing is to have fun. Now I call the first two teams to pitch number one. Good luck to everybody.

items.prompt: Where did the cooking class take place?
items.audio:
Last Saturday, my friend Zarina invited me to a cooking class in the old part of Bukhara, and I want to tell you about it, because it was one of the best mornings I have had this year.

The class took place in a small courtyard with a vine growing over the roof. The teacher was an elderly man called Ustoz Karim, who has been cooking plov for more than fifty years. He wore a white apron and spoke very slowly, with a lot of jokes. There were nine students, including two tourists from Germany and a young couple from Almaty.

First, Ustoz Karim showed us the ingredients. He said that the secret of a good plov is not any magic spice but the quality of the rice, the carrots and the oil. We needed one kilo of rice, one and a half kilos of yellow carrots, one kilo of lamb, three onions, a whole head of garlic and a handful of dried barberries. He insisted that the rice should be washed seven times, until the water becomes completely clear, and then left in warm salty water for an hour.

Then we started to cook in a huge black cauldron over a wood fire. We heated the oil until it smoked a little, fried the onions until they were golden brown, and added the meat. After that came the carrots, cut into long thin sticks. My sticks were a bit thick, and Ustoz Karim smiled and said that they were brave carrots. We added water and spices, and let everything simmer slowly for about forty minutes to make the rich base called zirvak.

Next we added the rice carefully, so that it did not mix with the base, pushed the garlic into the middle and covered the cauldron. The most difficult part was patience. We waited another thirty minutes without opening the lid.

At last we mixed the plov on a big round plate and sat down together at a long table in the courtyard. The Germans said it was the tastiest dish of their holiday. We ate, laughed and drank green tea until the afternoon. Before leaving, each of us received a small certificate and a recipe card. I am planning to cook plov for my parents next week.

items.prompt: Where does Eldor live?
items.audio:
Hello, and welcome to the Morning Commute podcast. Today's story is about a man named Eldor Hasanov, who decided to leave his car at home and cycle to work every day for a whole year.

Eldor lives in Tashkent and works in an insurance office about eleven kilometres from his flat. For years he drove there, and every morning he sat in traffic for nearly fifty minutes. He often arrived angry and tired, and he had gained almost ten kilos. One autumn day his doctor told him that his blood pressure was too high and that he needed to move more.

He bought a second-hand bicycle from a colleague for a very fair price and began riding on Mondays only. The first week was painful. His legs hurt, he was out of breath on every small hill, and he arrived at the office completely wet from sweat. But after a month he noticed that the journey took only thirty-five minutes, which was faster than driving. He also discovered a quiet route along a canal, away from the main road, with trees and even a few ducks.

By the end of winter he was cycling five days a week, even in light snow. He bought warm gloves, a bright jacket, and lights for the front and the back of the bike. His boss, impressed, arranged a safe place to keep bicycles in the office basement and a small shower for staff. Soon three other colleagues joined him, and they started a small group called the Wheel Team.

After twelve months Eldor had lost eleven kilos, his blood pressure was normal, and he had saved a lot of money on petrol and parking. He says that the biggest surprise was how much happier he felt. He no longer arrived at work stressed, because the ride cleared his mind.

Of course, there were some problems. Twice he got a flat tyre, and once a car almost hit him at a crossroads. For this reason he insists that every cyclist wears a helmet and follows the traffic rules.

His advice is to start slowly, choose a safe route, and look for friends to ride with. As he says, every journey begins with the first push on the pedals.

items.prompt: What is Sevara's job?
items.audio:
This is the story of how my sister Sevara finally joined a gym, told as she told it to me over dinner last Friday.

Sevara had been thinking about it for months. She works long hours as an accountant, and she wanted to feel stronger and less tired. One day a leaflet arrived in her letterbox, advertising a new fitness centre only ten minutes from her home. She called the number at the bottom and spoke to a young man named Timur.

Timur explained that the centre had three types of membership. The basic one cost three hundred thousand sum a month and allowed use of the gym and the changing rooms. The standard one cost four hundred thousand and included group classes, such as yoga and dance. The premium one, at six hundred thousand, also gave access to a swimming pool and a sauna. Sevara asked whether she could try before paying, and Timur said that every new client could have one free day.

The next evening she went there with her friend Madina. A trainer named Olga showed them around and explained how each machine worked. Olga asked Sevara about her goals, and Sevara said that she mostly wanted to improve her back and sleep better. Olga wrote a simple plan for three sessions a week, each lasting about an hour. It included ten minutes of warming up, thirty minutes of exercises with light weights, and a long stretch at the end.

Sevara was surprised how much she enjoyed the dance class that followed. The teacher played loud music, and for forty minutes nobody thought about work. She went home exhausted but happy. In the end she chose the standard membership and paid for three months in advance, which gave her a small discount.

After six weeks, she told me, her back hurts much less, and she falls asleep faster. The hardest part, she says, is still leaving the house on cold evenings. To help herself she packs her sports bag the night before and leaves it by the door.

Madina, however, stopped going after two weeks, and Sevara thinks that this is because she had no clear plan. So her main advice is to ask a trainer to write one for you.

The standard one cost four hundred thousand and included group classes, such as yoga and dance. The premium one, at six hundred thousand, also gave access to a swimming pool and a sauna. Sevara asked whether she could try before paying, and Timur said that every new client could have one free day.

The next evening she went there with her friend Madina. A trainer named Olga showed them around and explained how each machine worked. items.prompt: What percentage of the body is water?
items.audio:
Hello and welcome to Healthy Habits. I am your host, Nilufar, and in today's short programme we are going to talk about the simplest health advice in the world: drink more water.

Our bodies are about sixty percent water. We use it to control our temperature, to move food through the stomach, and to carry oxygen around the body. Even a small loss of water can make us feel tired, give us headaches, and make it harder to concentrate. A study among office workers found that people who drank two glasses of water in the morning solved problems faster than those who drank none.

How much do we actually need? There is no magic number, but most experts suggest about two litres a day for an adult. You will need more if the weather is hot, if you play sports, or if you are ill with a fever. You also get some water from your food. Watermelon, cucumbers, soup and oranges contain a lot of it.

Many of my listeners tell me that they simply forget to drink. Here are some tricks that work well. Keep a bottle on your desk where you can see it. Drink a glass when you wake up and another before each meal. Add a slice of lemon or a few leaves of mint if plain water is boring. Use a phone app that reminds you every two hours. Some people even choose a bottle with times written on its side, which shows how much you should have finished by noon and by evening.

A word about other drinks. Sweet fizzy drinks and packaged juices contain a large amount of sugar, and a single can may have seven spoons of it. Coffee and tea count partly, but too much caffeine can make you lose sleep. Energy drinks are best avoided completely, especially by young people.

How can you check that you are drinking enough? Look at the colour of your urine. It should be pale yellow. If it is dark, you need more water.

On next week's programme we will talk to a dietitian about healthy snacks for school children. Until then, take care, and do not forget your glass of water.

items.prompt: What was Kamola's job five years ago?
items.audio:
Good evening, and welcome to our weekly wellbeing talk. I am Kamola Yusupova, a yoga teacher, and tonight I would like to tell you how yoga helped me to deal with stress, and how it can help you.

Five years ago I was working as a manager in a large bank in Tashkent. I left home at seven in the morning and came back after nine in the evening. I slept badly, I had constant headaches, and I shouted at my family for small things. One weekend my neighbour invited me to a beginners' yoga class in a nearby park. I almost refused, because I thought yoga was only for people who could touch their toes. But she insisted, and I went.

The class was gentle and slow. The teacher, a calm woman in her sixties, began by asking us to close our eyes and simply notice our breathing. For the first time in weeks I felt my shoulders drop. After the class I slept for ten hours without waking up.

I started to go twice a week. Gradually I learned that yoga is not about being flexible. It is about connecting your movement with your breath. When you hold a pose and breathe slowly, your heart rate falls and your brain releases chemicals that make you feel calm. Scientists have measured this effect in many studies.

After a year, I made a big decision. I reduced my hours at the bank, and I trained to become a teacher. Now I work three days at the bank and teach yoga on the other days, and I have never been happier.

If you would like to try yoga, here are my tips. Choose a class for beginners and tell the teacher about any injuries. Wear comfortable clothes, and practise on an empty stomach, or at least two hours after a meal. Do not compare yourself to other people. And even at home, five minutes of slow breathing in the evening is enough to start.

Now I invite everybody to stand, take a mat from the pile at the back, and join me for a short, gentle session. Please place your mats about one metre apart.

items.prompt: Which radio station is reporting?
items.audio:
Hello, this is Feruza Mirzaeva, reporting for Radio Fergana from the Saturday farmers market in the centre of town. The sun is shining, the stalls are full of colour, and the smell of fresh bread is everywhere.

This market has been open every weekend for nearly fifteen years, but this season it has become bigger than ever. There are more than ninety stalls, and many of the sellers are small farmers who drive in from villages in the hills early in the morning. I spoke with Abdulla Qosimov, who sells apples, pears and dried fruit. He explained that this year his apples are especially sweet because the summer was dry and warm. A kilo costs eight thousand sum, and he said that he gives a free apple to every child who passes his stall.

Next to him I met a young woman called Dildora, who sells goat cheese and yoghurt. She learned the recipe from her grandmother and makes everything in a small kitchen at home. She told me that her customers like her cheese because it has no chemicals and no preservatives, and she showed me a small piece with herbs. I tried it, and it was delicious.

On the other side of the market there is a corner for bakers. A man named Otabek was taking hot flatbread out of a clay oven called a tandoor. He said that he starts work at three in the morning and bakes about four hundred loaves before the market opens. People were queuing to buy them while they were still warm.

The market also organises activities for families. Today there is a cooking show with a local chef at eleven o'clock, and an art workshop for children at noon, where they will paint pictures using vegetables. There is also a small box at the entrance where visitors can leave unwanted food for people in need.

A practical tip for shoppers: bring your own cloth bag, because the market has stopped giving out plastic ones this year. Come early for the best choice, and bargain politely. It is part of the tradition.

The market is open until three in the afternoon. This is Feruza Mirzaeva, and now it is back to the studio.

items.prompt: How long did the trip last?
items.audio:
Last August, six friends and I went on a three-day hiking trip in the Chimgan mountains, and I would like to tell you how it went, because we learned several useful lessons.

We met at the bus station at five in the morning. Our leader was Akmal, an experienced climber who works as a mountain guide. He checked our bags and made us leave behind anything unnecessary. My rucksack, for example, contained a heavy book and three extra pairs of jeans, and Akmal just shook his head. In the end my bag weighed nine kilos, which was still too heavy for me.

The first day was easy. We followed a path through a forest of walnut trees and stopped by a river for lunch. We had bread, boiled eggs, cheese and tomatoes, and we washed everything down with cold, clear water from the stream. By the afternoon we reached the first camp, at an altitude of about two thousand metres. We put up our tents, collected firewood and cooked a big pot of soup. In the evening the sky was full of stars, and Akmal told us stories about wolves and snow leopards.

On the second day the weather changed. Dark clouds came over the ridge, and a cold wind began to blow. Akmal decided to leave early to avoid rain at the top. The climb was steep, and my knees hurt, but the view from the pass was unforgettable. We could see a blue lake far below and, behind it, mountains with snow on the tops. Unfortunately, halfway down it started to rain, and the path became slippery. One of us, Lola, fell and hurt her ankle. Akmal quickly bandaged it with a first aid kit and shared the weight of her bag between the rest of us.

We arrived at the second camp wet and tired, but a hot meal and a dry sleeping bag made everything better.

On the last morning we walked slowly back to the road, where a minibus was waiting. Lola's ankle was swollen, but she was smiling.

What did I learn? Always bring proper boots, a waterproof jacket and a first aid kit. Pack light. Listen to your guide. And never ignore a weather forecast.

Last August, six friends and I went on a three-day hiking trip in the Chimgan mountains, and I would like to tell you how it went, because we learned several useful lessons.

We met at the bus station at five in the morning. Our leader was Akmal, an experienced climber who works as a mountain guide. He checked our bags and made us leave behind anything unnecessary. My rucksack, for example, contained a heavy book and three extra pairs of jeans, and Akmal just shook his head. In the end my bag weighed nine kilos, which was still too heavy for me.

The first day was easy. We followed a path through a forest of walnut trees and stopped by a river for lunch. We had bread, boiled eggs, cheese and tomatoes, and we washed everything down with cold, clear water from the stream. By the afternoon we reached the first camp, at an altitude of about two thousand metres. We put up our tents, collected firewood and cooked a big pot of soup. In the evening the sky was full of stars, and Akmal told us stories about wolves and snow leopards.

On the second day the weather changed. Dark clouds came over the ridge, and a cold wind began to blow. Akmal decided to leave early to avoid rain at the top. The climb was steep, and my knees hurt, but the view from the pass was unforgettable. We could see a blue lake far below and, behind it, mountains with snow on the tops. Unfortunately, halfway down it started to rain, and the path became slippery. One of us, Lola, fell and hurt her ankle. Akmal quickly bandaged it with a first aid kit and shared the weight of her bag between the rest of us.

We arrived at the second camp wet and tired, but a hot meal and a dry sleeping bag made everything better.

On the last morning we walked slowly back to the road, where a minibus was waiting. Lola's ankle was swollen, but she was smiling.

What did I learn? Always bring proper boots, a waterproof jacket and a first aid kit. Pack light. Listen to your guide. And never ignore a weather forecast.

items.prompt: What is Doctor Ergashev's profession?
items.audio:
Good morning, children, and good morning to the teachers and parents too. My name is Doctor Sanjar Ergashev, and I am a dentist. Today I am going to talk about your teeth, and I promise that it will not hurt at all.

Let me start with a question. How many teeth do adults have? The answer is thirty-two. And how many do you have right now? Most of you have about twenty, because you are still losing your baby teeth. This is completely normal. But the new teeth that grow in place of them must last you for the rest of your lives, so it is very important to take good care of them.

What is the enemy of teeth? Sugar. When you eat sweets, small bacteria in your mouth feed on the sugar and make acid. This acid slowly makes tiny holes in your teeth. We call them cavities. The longer sugar stays on your teeth, the more damage it does. That is why it is better to eat a whole cake at one time, and then clean your teeth, than to eat a biscuit every half hour all day.

Now, I am not saying that you should never eat sweets. Of course you can have a piece of chocolate with your friends. But remember these simple rules. First, brush your teeth twice a day, for two minutes each time, in the morning and before bed. Second, use a soft brush and a toothpaste with fluoride, which makes your teeth stronger. Third, change your toothbrush every three months. Fourth, drink water after sweet food. Fifth, visit the dentist at least once every six months, even if nothing hurts.

Some foods are friends of your teeth. Cheese, for example, helps to remove acid. Crunchy vegetables like carrots and cucumbers clean your teeth as you chew. Milk gives you calcium, which builds strong bones and teeth.

I have brought some models of teeth and big toothbrushes, so everybody will have a chance to practise. In a few minutes I will call volunteers to come to the front. At the end, each child will get a small gift: a toothbrush in your favourite colour and a sticker that says that you are a Tooth Hero. Who is ready to begin?

Good morning, children, and good morning to the teachers and parents too. My name is Doctor Sanjar Ergashev, and I am a dentist. Today I am going to talk about your teeth, and I promise that it will not hurt at all.

Let me start with a question. How many teeth do adults have? The answer is thirty-two. And how many do you have right now? Most of you have about twenty, because you are still losing your baby teeth. This is completely normal. But the new teeth that grow in place of them must last you for the rest of your lives, so it is very important to take good care of them.

What is the enemy of teeth? Sugar. When you eat sweets, small bacteria in your mouth feed on the sugar and make acid. This acid slowly makes tiny holes in your teeth. We call them cavities. The longer sugar stays on your teeth, the more damage it does. That is why it is better to eat a whole cake at one time, and then clean your teeth, than to eat a biscuit every half hour all day.

Now, I am not saying that you should never eat sweets. Of course you can have a piece of chocolate with your friends. But remember these simple rules. First, brush your teeth twice a day, for two minutes each time, in the morning and before bed. Second, use a soft brush and a toothpaste with fluoride, which makes your teeth stronger. Third, change your toothbrush every three months. Fourth, drink water after sweet food. Fifth, visit the dentist at least once every six months, even if nothing hurts.

Some foods are friends of your teeth. Cheese, for example, helps to remove acid. Crunchy vegetables like carrots and cucumbers clean your teeth as you chew. Milk gives you calcium, which builds strong bones and teeth.

I have brought some models of teeth and big toothbrushes, so everybody will have a chance to practise. In a few minutes I will call volunteers to come to the front. At the end, each child will get a small gift: a toothbrush in your favourite colour and a sticker that says that you are a Tooth Hero. Who is ready to begin?

items.prompt: Why did Dilnoza call the helpline?
items.audio:
Good morning, and welcome to the Tashkent Phone Clinic helpline. This is a story about a phone call that one of our customers made last week, and we are sharing it because many people ask us the same questions. The customer was a student called Dilnoza, and she rang us at nine in the morning because her smartphone had fallen from her desk and the screen had cracked across the middle.

The technician who answered was a friendly man named Bobur. He asked Dilnoza a few simple questions. First, he wanted to know whether the phone still turned on. She said that it did, but the touch screen only worked on the left side. Then he asked how old the phone was. Dilnoza explained that she had bought it nearly two years ago, so the guarantee had already finished. Bobur told her not to worry, because the shop offered a repair service that cost much less than a new phone.

Bobur explained that a new screen for her model would cost about eighty dollars, and that the work would take roughly one hour. However, the shop did not have the part in stock, so they had to order it from a supplier in Samarkand. The part would arrive on Thursday afternoon, which meant that Dilnoza could collect her phone on Friday morning. She was a little disappointed because she had an important online exam on Wednesday and needed her phone for the video call.

To help her, Bobur suggested a temporary solution. The shop could lend her an old phone for three days, free of charge, as long as she left a small deposit. Dilnoza liked this idea very much. Before ending the call, Bobur gave her some advice. He told her to back up all her photos and messages to the cloud before bringing the phone in, because repairs sometimes delete data by accident. He also recommended buying a strong protective case and a glass cover, which together cost about ten dollars.

Dilnoza thanked him, wrote down the address on Navoi Street, and promised to visit that same afternoon. She arrived at four o'clock, signed a short form, and left with the borrowed phone. On Friday she returned, paid for the repair, and was delighted that her own phone looked brand new again. She even bought the protective case, and she says she will never leave her phone near the edge of a desk again.

items.prompt: How long has Aziz worked with battery technology?
items.audio:
Welcome back to Morning Science, the programme that explains the modern world in simple words. Today we are talking about electric cars, and our guest is an engineer named Aziz Karimov, who has worked with battery technology for twelve years. Aziz, thank you for joining us.

The host begins by asking why electric cars have become so popular recently. Aziz answers that there are three main reasons. First, the batteries are much cheaper than they were ten years ago. Second, many cities now have charging stations, so drivers feel safer on long journeys. Third, people are more worried about pollution and want cleaner transport. He says that in some countries, nearly half of the new cars sold last year were electric.

The host then asks about the biggest problem. Aziz explains that the most common complaint is the driving range. A typical family car can travel about four hundred kilometres on one full charge, but in very cold weather the distance can fall by a quarter. Charging also takes longer than filling a petrol tank. At a fast charging station, a battery reaches eighty percent in about thirty minutes, but at home it can take the whole night.

Next, the host mentions the price. Aziz agrees that electric cars are still more expensive to buy, but he adds that they are cheaper to run. Electricity costs less than fuel, and the engine has fewer moving parts, so there is less to repair. Over five years, he says, a driver can save several thousand dollars. He also points out that governments often give tax benefits to people who choose electric vehicles.

The last question is about the environment. Aziz is honest and says that making the battery produces a lot of carbon dioxide, and mining the metals can harm nature. However, after about two years of driving, the electric car becomes cleaner than a petrol car. Companies are also learning to reuse old batteries, for example to store energy in houses.

To finish, the host asks for advice. Aziz says that anyone who drives short distances every day should seriously think about an electric car, but people who often travel through remote villages should wait until charging stations are everywhere. Thank you, Aziz, and now let us listen to some music.

items.prompt: How far from the Earth does the telescope orbit?
items.answer: About one and a half million kilometres
items.audio:
In this week's science interview, a reporter named Laura Bennett speaks with Doctor Malika Rahimova, an astronomer who works with a large space telescope. Laura begins by asking what makes this telescope special. Malika explains that it orbits the Earth about one and a half million kilometres away, so it is far from the light and heat of our planet. Its main mirror is made of eighteen golden pieces, and together they are more than six metres wide.

Laura asks how long it took to build. Malika laughs and says that the project lasted more than twenty years. Many teams in different countries worked on it, and there were several delays because the engineers had to test every tiny part. The launch finally took place on a cold winter morning, and Malika says that she watched it with her colleagues and cried with happiness when the rocket left the ground.

Then Laura asks what the telescope looks at. Malika says that it studies very old light from the first stars and galaxies, which travelled for billions of years before reaching us. It can also look at the atmosphere of planets around other stars, and scientists hope to find signs of water. In one recent observation, the telescope discovered a planet that is roughly the size of Earth, although it is much too hot for any life.

Laura wants to know about the pictures, which have been in many newspapers. Malika explains that the telescope does not see colours the way human eyes do. It collects infrared light, which is invisible, and then scientists change it into colours so that people can understand the images. She emphasises that the colours are not false, because they show real differences in temperature and material.

Finally, Laura asks about the future. Malika says that the telescope has enough fuel to work for about twenty years, and she is already planning a project to study a cloud of gas near a young star. She also enjoys visiting schools, because she believes that children who look at these pictures may become the scientists of tomorrow. Laura thanks her, and says that she will never look at the night sky in the same way again.
options: About one and a half million kilometres

items.prompt: How long did Sevara's experiment last?
items.audio:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to Digital Life, the podcast about how technology changes our daily habits. My name is Sevara, and today I want to tell you about an experiment that I did last month. I decided to stop using social media for thirty days, and I would like to share what I learned.

The idea started one evening when I noticed that I had spent nearly four hours on my phone without doing anything useful. I checked the screen time report and found that I opened my favourite photo app about ninety times a day. That frightened me a little, so I deleted five apps and told my friends that I would be difficult to reach.

The first week was the hardest. I kept picking up my phone out of habit, even when there were no notifications. I felt bored on the bus and nervous during lunch. My brother Jamshid laughed at me and said that I behaved like someone who had given up sweets. However, by the end of the week, I noticed that I was sleeping better, probably because I no longer looked at the screen in bed.

During the second and third weeks, I discovered new ways to spend my time. I finished two books, I cooked a traditional dish with my grandmother, and I joined a small running club that meets every Saturday at seven in the morning. I also found that I remembered conversations better, because I was really listening to people instead of thinking about what to post.

Of course, the experiment was not perfect. I missed some important news, such as the birthday party of a cousin, and I felt lonely when my friends talked about funny videos that I had not seen. Also, my work as a designer needs social media a little, so I had to use one account for twenty minutes every Monday.

At the end of the month, I did not go back to my old habits. Now I use only two apps, and I limit myself to one hour a day. My advice is simple. You do not need to quit forever, but try a short break and see how you feel. Thank you for listening, and see you next week.

items.prompt: What is the topic of Professor Yusupova's talk?
items.audio:
Good morning, everybody. I am Professor Nodira Yusupova, and today I would like to speak about one of the biggest problems of our time, which is plastic waste. I will explain where it comes from, why it is dangerous, and how science is helping us to solve it.

Let us begin with some numbers. Every year, people produce about four hundred million tonnes of plastic. A large part of it is used only once, for example in bags, bottles and food packages. Less than one fifth is recycled, and the rest ends up in rubbish dumps, in rivers and finally in the sea. A plastic bottle needs about four hundred and fifty years to disappear completely, which is much longer than a human life.

Why is this dangerous? Large pieces of plastic can trap or kill animals such as turtles and birds. But the smaller pieces are even more worrying. Over time, the sun and the waves break plastic into tiny parts called microplastics. Fish swallow them, and then they can reach our dinner table. Scientists have even found microplastics in drinking water and in the blood of some people, although we still do not know exactly how harmful they are.

Now for the good news. Researchers have discovered a bacterium in a rubbish dump that can eat a certain kind of plastic. In my laboratory, we are testing similar organisms, and in a few years they may help to clean large amounts of waste. Another team has invented a method that turns old bottles into fuel, and a third group produces clothing from recycled plastic.

However, technology alone is not enough. We must also change our habits. I recommend three simple steps. First, carry your own cloth bag when you go shopping. Second, choose a metal bottle instead of buying water in plastic. Third, sort your rubbish at home, because clean plastic is much easier to recycle.

Finally, I invite you to join our university project. Next month, our students will clean the banks of the Chirchiq River, and we need about two hundred volunteers. If you are interested, please leave your email at the table by the door. Thank you very much for your attention.

items.prompt: What is Rustam's job?
items.audio:
This is the story of a phone call that took place on a rainy Tuesday afternoon between a customer called Rustam and the support team of a computer company. Rustam is a young accountant, and his laptop had stopped working only five months after he bought it. He was upset, because he had an important report to finish by Friday.

The support agent was a patient woman called Gulnora. She greeted him politely and asked for the serial number, which is printed on the bottom of the laptop. Rustam turned the machine over and read the long number slowly. Gulnora then asked him to describe the problem. He explained that the screen suddenly became black while he was working, and that after that the laptop would not start, although a small green light was on.

Gulnora asked him to try a few simple things. First, she told him to disconnect the charger and remove all the cables and memory sticks. Then she asked him to hold the power button for fifteen seconds. Rustam did everything carefully, but the laptop still did not respond. Next, she suggested connecting the charger again and waiting for ten minutes. Unfortunately, nothing changed.

At this point, Gulnora said that the problem was probably in the battery or the main board. Because the laptop was still under guarantee, which lasted for two years, the repair would be free. She offered two choices. Rustam could send the laptop by post, and the company would repair it within seven working days, or he could take it to a service centre in his city, where the repair might be done in three days. Rustam chose the second option because of his deadline.

Before finishing, Gulnora gave him a reference number and sent a confirmation message to his phone. She also reminded him to bring his receipt and a copy of his passport. Rustam thanked her and said that he was surprised by how polite and clear the service was. On Wednesday morning he took the laptop to the centre, and on Friday it was ready. He finished his report that evening, only two hours before the deadline.

The support agent was a patient woman called Gulnora. She greeted him politely and asked for the serial number, which is printed on the bottom of the laptop. Rustam turned the machine over and read the long number slowly. Gulnora then asked him to describe the problem. He explained that the screen suddenly became black while he was working, and that after that the laptop would not start, although a small green light was on.

Gulnora asked him to try a few simple things. First, she told him to disconnect the charger and remove all the cables and memory sticks. Then she asked him to hold the power button for fifteen seconds. Rustam did everything carefully, but the laptop still did not respond. Next, she suggested connecting the charger again and waiting for ten minutes. Unfortunately, nothing changed.

At this point, Gulnora said that the problem was probably in the battery or the main board. Because the laptop was still under guarantee, which lasted for two years, the repair would be free. She offered two choices. Rustam could send the laptop by post, and the company would repair it within seven working days, or he could take it to a service centre in his city, where the repair might be done in three days. Rustam chose the second option because of his deadline.

Before finishing, Gulnora gave him a reference number and sent a confirmation message to his phone. She also reminded him to bring his receipt and a copy of his passport. Rustam thanked her and said that he was surprised by how polite and clear the service was. On Wednesday morning he took the laptop to the centre, and on Friday it was ready. He finished his report that evening, only two hours before the deadline.

items.prompt: Where is Timur's studio?
items.audio:
Hello, and welcome to Creative Corner on Radio Youth. Today we are speaking about a job that many young listeners dream about: designing video games. Our guest is Timur Alimov, who started a small studio in Bukhara four years ago, and who has just released his first game. Timur, congratulations.

Timur thanks the host and says that he first became interested in games at the age of eleven, when his uncle gave him an old computer. He did not only play. He wanted to understand how everything worked, so he read free books online and watched tutorials in the evenings. At sixteen he made a very simple game about a cat that collects fish, and he shared it with friends.

The host asks how a game is made. Timur explains that a team usually includes several kinds of specialists. The programmers write the code, the artists draw the characters and the world, and the sound designers record music and effects. There is also a writer who creates the story. In his studio there are only six people, so everyone has to do more than one job. He himself draws the maps and tests the levels.

The new game is called Silk Road Runner. The player controls a young merchant who travels between ancient cities and must avoid thieves and sandstorms. It took two years to finish and cost about thirty thousand dollars, which Timur saved from a previous job and a small loan. He says that the hardest part was balancing the difficulty, because the game must not be too easy or too frustrating.

The host asks about advice for beginners. Timur says that you should start with a tiny project and finish it, rather than dreaming about a huge adventure. He also advises learning English, because most tools and communities use it. Finally, he suggests showing your work to other people early and listening to their opinions.

To end, Timur mentions that the game is available for free for the first week, and that more than ten thousand people have already downloaded it. The host wishes him luck, and we now continue with our programme.

items.prompt: How long has Karim studied the weather?
items.audio:
In today's programme we are visiting the national weather centre, where we meet Doctor Karim Saidov, a climate scientist who has studied the weather for more than twenty years. Karim, thank you for inviting us. Please tell us how a forecast is made.

Karim explains that the process begins with information. Thousands of weather stations around the world measure temperature, wind and rain every hour. Satellites in space take pictures of clouds, and ships and aeroplanes also send their measurements. items.prompt: When does the course start?
items.answer: On the first Monday of September
items.audio:
Hello, and thank you for calling the Future Coders Academy information line. This recorded message gives you all the details about our new course for beginners, which starts on the first Monday of September. Please listen to the end, because we explain how to register and what you need to bring.

The course is called Programming from Zero, and it is designed for people who have never written a single line of code. It lasts for four months, and classes take place three times a week, on Monday, Wednesday and Friday, from six to eight in the evening. This schedule suits students and people who work during the day. Every group has a maximum of fifteen learners, so that the teacher can help each person.

During the first month, you will learn the basic ideas of programming using a friendly language called Python. In the second month, you will build small programs, such as a calculator and a quiz. In the third month, you will learn how websites work and create your own page. In the final month, each learner will work on a personal project and present it to the class. Our best projects are shown to local companies, and several graduates have already found jobs.

The teachers are experienced developers who work in the industry. The main teacher is Madina Ergasheva, who has spent nine years in a software company in Tashkent. She believes that anyone can learn to code with practice and patience. Every lesson includes a short lecture and a long practical part, when students write code on their own computers. The academy has twenty modern computers, but you are welcome to bring your own laptop.

The price of the whole course is four hundred and fifty dollars, and you can pay in three parts. Students under twenty-one receive a discount of twenty percent. To register, visit our website or come to the office on Amir Temur Avenue, which is open every day except Sunday from nine to five. You will also need a copy of your passport and a recent photograph. If you have more questions, please stay on the line, and one of our advisers will speak to you soon. Thank you for your interest.
options: On the first Monday of September
On the last Friday of August

items.prompt: What is Farhod's job?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, students. My name is Farhod Tursunov, and I work as a computer security specialist. Today I have been asked to talk to you for half an hour about staying safe on the internet. I will not use difficult words, and I hope that you will remember at least three things from my talk.

Let me start with a short story. Last year, a friend of mine received an email that seemed to come from his bank. It said that his account had a problem and asked him to click on a link and enter his password. Luckily, he noticed that the address of the sender had a small mistake, with one letter missing. This kind of trick is called phishing, and criminals send millions of such messages every day. If you are not sure, never click. Instead, open your bank's official website yourself or call the number on your card.

The second topic is passwords. Many people choose simple passwords, like their name and a birth year, because they are easy to remember. Unfortunately, they are also easy to guess. A good password is long, at least twelve characters, and mixes letters, numbers and symbols. Even better, use a short sentence that only you know. Of course, you should use a different password for every account. If this sounds impossible, use a password manager, which is a safe programme that remembers everything for you.

Third, I recommend two step verification. This means that after you type your password, the website sends a code to your phone. Even if a thief learns your password, he cannot enter without the code. It takes only one extra minute, and it protects you very well.

Fourth, be careful with public wireless networks in cafes and airports. Avoid shopping or banking when you are connected to them. Also, keep your phone and computer updated, because updates often repair security holes.

Finally, think before you share. Photos, addresses and holiday plans can be used by strangers. If something is too good to be true, such as a free phone for answering a survey, it is almost certainly a trap. Thank you for listening, and now I am happy to answer your questions.

items.prompt: What is Zarina's latest film about?
items.audio:
Welcome to Media Matters. In today's episode, our reporter Anvar speaks with Zarina Hamidova, a documentary film maker whose latest film about the Aral Sea has just won a prize at an international festival. Zarina, congratulations.

Anvar begins by asking how the idea started. Zarina explains that her grandfather used to live in a fishing village on the coast. As a child she listened to his stories about boats and fish, and later she saw photographs of the same place, where old ships stand in the desert. She says that the contrast was so strong that she decided to tell this story to the world.

Anvar asks about the work. Zarina says that the film took three years. The team travelled by car for two thousand kilometres and spent nearly a hundred days in the region. They interviewed forty people, including old fishermen, doctors and young scientists. The crew consisted of only five people, so they had to carry equipment on their own. The hardest moment was a dust storm that damaged one of their cameras, but they borrowed another from a local school.

They then talk about technology. Zarina explains that modern cameras are small and cheap, and that she even used a drone to film the dry sea bed from above. She edits the material on an ordinary laptop, and she shares short clips on social media to attract an audience. She believes that the internet has given independent film makers a great opportunity, because they no longer need a big television company.

Anvar asks what message she wants viewers to receive. Zarina says that the film is not only about sadness. It also shows hope, because new forests of special desert trees are growing on the dry sea bed, and some fish are returning to the northern part of the lake. She wants people to see that action is possible.

In the end, Anvar asks about her plans. Zarina says that she will rest for a month, and then begin a film about traditional musicians. The film about the sea can be watched online, free of charge, from next Monday. Thank you, Zarina.

items.prompt: In which region is the village?
items.audio:
Good evening, and welcome to the Green Planet report. Tonight we travel to a small village in the Navoi region, called Oltin Qishloq, where something remarkable has happened during the last year. The whole community now gets most of its electricity from the sun.

The project began when the village teacher, a woman named Shahnoza Ibragimova, noticed that the school often lost power in winter. The children could not use computers, and the classrooms were cold. She wrote a letter to an environmental organisation, and after several months it agreed to help. The organisation paid for sixty solar panels, which were placed on the roofs of the school, the clinic and the village shop.

The installation took only three weeks. Two engineers came from the city to train local young people, and six villagers learned how to clean and repair the panels. One of them, a nineteen year old called Sardor, says that the work is interesting and that he now wants to study energy at university. He explains that the panels produce more electricity in summer, when the days are long, and that extra power is stored in big batteries for the night.

The results are impressive. Before the project, the village paid about two hundred dollars every month for electricity, and now it pays less than fifty. The money that is saved is used to buy books and a new refrigerator for the clinic, where doctors can now keep medicine safely. The school has a small computer room, and in the evenings adults come to learn how to use the internet.

Of course, there are still some difficulties. On cloudy days the power is lower, and the batteries are expensive, so they must be replaced every ten years. However, the villagers are not worried. They plan to add a small wind generator next spring.

Other villages have already asked for advice, and Shahnoza has promised to visit them. She believes that solar energy is not a luxury, but a practical solution for places far from the big power lines. That is all for tonight, and we will see you next week.

items.prompt: What is Behzod's job?
items.audio:
Let me tell you about a phone call that my neighbour Behzod made to his internet company last Sunday. Behzod works from home as a translator, and on Sunday morning his connection suddenly became very slow. Pages needed several minutes to open, and a video meeting with a client in London was planned for noon. He called the support number and waited for about six minutes before a young man answered.

The agent introduced himself as Otabek and asked Behzod for his address and the name on the account. Then he asked whether the problem was in one device or in all of them. Behzod said that his phone, his laptop and even his television were slow. Otabek replied that this usually means that the fault is in the router or in the line, not in a single machine.

Otabek asked Behzod to look at the router and describe the lights. Behzod saw that the light with a small globe was red instead of green. Otabek explained that this meant the router had lost contact with the main network. He asked Behzod to switch the router off, wait for thirty seconds, and switch it on again. Behzod did so, but after five minutes the light was still red.

Otabek then checked the system and discovered that there was a problem in the whole district, because a cable had been damaged during road works near the market. He apologised and said that engineers were already repairing it, and that the service should return within three hours. As a gesture of kindness, the company would reduce the monthly bill by ten percent.

Behzod was worried about his meeting, so Otabek suggested a solution. He could use his mobile phone as a hotspot, and the company would give him an extra five gigabytes of data for free. Behzod accepted gladly. The meeting at noon went smoothly, even though the picture was not perfect, and the home connection came back at two thirty. Behzod told me that he was impressed, because the agent was honest and helpful, and he did not feel angry at all.

items.prompt: What is Doctor Rakhmonov's speciality?
items.audio:
Good evening, ladies and gentlemen. I am Doctor Sanjar Rakhmonov, a heart specialist, and tonight I would like to explain how artificial intelligence is beginning to change the work of hospitals. I will give you three examples and then talk about some worries.

The first example is the reading of medical pictures. Every day, a radiologist looks at hundreds of x rays and scans, and tiredness can cause mistakes. In our hospital, we have been testing a programme that studies these pictures first and marks any strange areas. Last year it helped our doctors to find small signs of lung disease in forty patients, much earlier than usual. Of course, the final decision always belongs to a human doctor.

The second example concerns waiting time. Our emergency department used to be very crowded, especially on Friday evenings. Now a computer system predicts how many patients will arrive, based on the weather, the date and past records. Managers can then call extra nurses in advance. As a result, the average waiting time has fallen from ninety minutes to fifty.

The third example is a small device that people wear on the wrist. It measures the heartbeat and can warn the owner if the rhythm becomes dangerous. One of my own patients, a retired driver named Ulugbek, received such a warning at night, came to the hospital at once, and received treatment in time. He says that the device saved his life.

Now, the worries. First, these systems need a huge amount of personal information, and we must protect it carefully. Second, a programme can make mistakes if it was trained on data from only one group of people. Third, some patients fear that machines will replace the kindness of a doctor. I believe that this will not happen. A computer can calculate, but it cannot hold a frightened child's hand.

In conclusion, artificial intelligence is a powerful assistant, not a replacement. If we use it wisely, it will give doctors more time to speak with their patients. Thank you for listening, and I welcome your questions.

items.prompt: Who is Dilnoza Karimova?
items.answer: The head of the Eco Club
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the weekly announcements at Greenfield School. My name is Dilnoza Karimova, and I am the head of the Eco Club. Today I want to tell you about our new recycling project, which begins next Monday.

For many years our school has thrown away too much rubbish. Last term the cleaners counted the bags and found that we filled almost forty big bags every week, and nearly half of that was paper and plastic bottles. That is why the club has decided to act. From next Monday there will be three coloured bins in every classroom. The blue bin is for paper, the yellow bin is for plastic bottles and cans, and the green bin is for food waste from lunch. Please do not put food in the blue bin, because wet food makes the paper useless.

Every Friday, students from class eight will carry the full bins to the big containers behind the gym. A local company called CleanCity will collect them on Saturday morning and take them to a recycling centre outside town. The company has promised to pay the school a small amount of money for every ton of paper. We plan to use that money to buy ten young trees for the school garden.

Mister Rustam, our science teacher, will give a short lesson in each class on Tuesday to explain how the bins work. He will also show a film about what happens to a plastic bottle after it leaves our school. Some students asked if they can bring rubbish from home. The answer is no, because the containers are too small, but you can tell your families about the project and ask them to sort their own waste.

There will be a prize for the class that makes the least rubbish during the first month. The winners will have a picnic in the park with their teacher. Finally, the club needs six volunteers to help with posters. If you like drawing, please come to room twelve at lunchtime on Wednesday. Thank you for listening, and let us make our school cleaner together.

items.prompt: What part of our food depends on insects that carry pollen?
items.audio:
Welcome to Nature Hour on Radio Valley. I am Aziz Tursunov, and this afternoon we are talking about bees. Many people think of bees only as makers of honey, but their real job is much bigger. About one third of the food we eat depends on insects that carry pollen from flower to flower. Without bees, we would have fewer apples, almonds and cucumbers.

My guest today is Mary Collins, a beekeeper who has looked after bees in the north of England for twenty years. Mary says that the number of wild bees has fallen sharply, mostly because of farm chemicals and the loss of meadows. In her village, farmers used to leave wide strips of wild flowers beside the fields. Now many of those strips are gone, and the bees have to fly much farther to find food.

A healthy hive can contain fifty thousand bees in the summer, but in winter only about ten thousand stay alive, keeping the queen warm by shaking their bodies together. Mary explained that a worker bee lives for only six weeks in summer and visits hundreds of flowers every day. One small jar of honey needs the work of many bees during their whole lives.

I asked Mary what ordinary people can do. She gave three simple ideas. First, plant flowers on your balcony, such as lavender or sunflowers, because bees love them. Second, never use strong chemicals in your garden. Third, put a shallow dish of water with a few stones inside, so tired bees can land and drink safely.

She also warned listeners not to panic when a bee comes close. Bees rarely sting unless they feel in danger, and a bee that stings dies soon afterwards. Mary will visit our town next month and give a free workshop at the library on Saturday at ten in the morning. Children can try on the special white suits, and everyone will taste fresh honey. After the break we will hear from a listener, Gulnora, who started her own small hive on a roof in the city centre. Stay with us.

My guest today is Mary Collins, a beekeeper who has looked after bees in the north of England for twenty years. Mary says that the number of wild bees has fallen sharply, mostly because of farm chemicals and the loss of meadows. In her village, farmers used to leave wide strips of wild flowers beside the fields. Now many of those strips are gone, and the bees have to fly much farther to find food.

A healthy hive can contain fifty thousand bees in the summer, but in winter only about ten thousand stay alive, keeping the queen warm by shaking their bodies together. Mary explained that a worker bee lives for only six weeks in summer and visits hundreds of flowers every day. One small jar of honey needs the work of many bees during their whole lives.

Second, never use strong chemicals in your garden. Third, put a shallow dish of water with a few stones inside, so tired bees can land and drink safely.

items.prompt: Who lives beside the river?
items.audio:
Last Thursday evening Nodira received a phone call from her uncle Bakhrom, who lives in a small village beside the Chirchiq River. He sounded worried. Nodira asks him what is happening, and he answers that it has been raining heavily for three days and the river is rising fast. The water has already covered the road to the market, and the school has closed.

Nodira asks whether the family is safe. Bakhrom says that everyone is fine, but they moved the sheep and the two cows to the higher field behind the mosque. His wife Zulfiya packed a bag with documents, warm clothes, bread and bottles of clean water, in case the family has to leave at night.

Nodira asks if the local authorities have given any advice. Bakhrom says that a man from the emergency service came on a motorbike in the afternoon. He told the villagers to listen to the radio and to avoid walking near the riverbank. He also said that the bridge may be closed if the water rises another half metre.

Bakhrom explains that floods happen more often than before. When he was a boy, the river came over its banks only once in ten years, but now it happens almost every spring. Old people say that the mountains get less snow but more sudden rain, and the ground cannot hold the water because many trees on the hills were cut down.

Nodira offers to drive to the village on Friday morning with blankets and tinned food. Bakhrom thanks her but asks her to wait, because the road is too dangerous. Instead he suggests that she sends money to the village fund, which buys sandbags. They also talk about his young son Sardor, who was excited about the high water and wanted to go outside to see it. Bakhrom told him that the river is not a toy. At the end of the call, Nodira promises to phone again on Saturday at nine in the morning. She goes to bed late and listens to the weather forecast, hoping that the rain will stop soon.

items.prompt: What is Timur Aliyev's job?
items.audio:
Today we have an interview with Timur Aliyev, a park ranger in the Chatkal mountains. A reporter named Laura asks him about snow leopards. Timur answers that the snow leopard is one of the most secret animals on Earth. In ten years of work he has seen a wild one only four times.

Laura asks how many leopards live in the park. Timur says that scientists estimate about twenty, but nobody can be sure. Rangers count them using cameras that start when something moves. The cameras are fixed to rocks at a height of one metre, and the team checks them every three months.

Laura asks about the animal's body. Timur explains that its thick grey fur with dark spots is perfect camouflage on the rocks, and its long tail, almost as long as its body, helps it keep its balance on steep slopes. It also uses the tail like a scarf, wrapping it round its nose when it sleeps in the cold. A snow leopard can jump fifteen metres, which is about the length of a bus.

Laura wonders what the animals eat. Timur says they hunt wild goats and sheep, but when these become rare, leopards sometimes attack farm animals. That makes villagers angry, and some hunters kill the leopards. To solve this problem, the park built strong night shelters for sheep and gave them to twenty families. Since then, attacks have fallen by half.

Laura asks what tourists can do. Timur says that visitors should stay on the paths, take no plastic into the mountains, and never follow an animal for a photograph. He also invites young people to join the summer volunteer camp, which lasts two weeks in July and teaches how to read animal tracks. At the end, Laura asks if he is optimistic. Timur smiles and says yes, because every year the cameras show new baby leopards, and that is the best news a ranger can hear.

Today we have an interview with Timur Aliyev, a park ranger in the Chatkal mountains. A reporter named Laura asks him about snow leopards. Timur answers that the snow leopard is one of the most secret animals on Earth. In ten years of work he has seen a wild one only four times.

Laura asks how many leopards live in the park. Timur says that scientists estimate about twenty, but nobody can be sure. Rangers count them using cameras that start when something moves. The cameras are fixed to rocks at a height of one metre, and the team checks them every three months.

Laura asks about the animal's body. Timur explains that its thick grey fur with dark spots is perfect camouflage on the rocks, and its long tail, almost as long as its body, helps it keep its balance on steep slopes. It also uses the tail like a scarf, wrapping it round its nose when it sleeps in the cold. A snow leopard can jump fifteen metres, which is about the length of a bus.

Laura wonders what the animals eat. Timur says they hunt wild goats and sheep, but when these become rare, leopards sometimes attack farm animals. That makes villagers angry, and some hunters kill the leopards. To solve this problem, the park built strong night shelters for sheep and gave them to twenty families. Since then, attacks have fallen by half.

Laura asks what tourists can do. Timur says that visitors should stay on the paths, take no plastic into the mountains, and never follow an animal for a photograph. He also invites young people to join the summer volunteer camp, which lasts two weeks in July and teaches how to read animal tracks. At the end, Laura asks if he is optimistic. Timur smiles and says yes, because every year the cameras show new baby leopards, and that is the best news a ranger can hear.

items.prompt: When will the clean-up take place?
items.answer: On the second Sunday of June
items.audio:
Attention please, all residents of Seaview Bay. This is an announcement from the town council about the annual beach clean-up day, which will take place on the second Sunday of June. Everyone is welcome, young and old, and we hope to see more volunteers than ever before.

We will meet at eight in the morning next to the old lighthouse. Gloves and rubbish bags will be provided, but please bring your own bottle of water, a hat and sunscreen, because the sun on the beach can be very strong. Last year four hundred volunteers collected three tons of rubbish in just one morning. Most of it was plastic bottles, old fishing nets and cigarette ends, which are very dangerous for birds and fish.

This year we have some special guests. At eleven, a marine biologist, Doctor Helen Park, will give a short talk about how plastic harms seabirds. She will show photographs of birds that were saved by local volunteers, and she will answer questions from children. At noon, the Blue Wave cafe will give free lemonade and sandwiches to everyone who has helped. The owner, Mister Ismoil, says that the sea is the heart of our town and he wants to say thank you.

If you do not have a car, free buses will leave from the market square every thirty minutes between seven and eight. Children under ten must come with an adult, and groups from schools should tell their teachers in advance. The clean-up will finish at two in the afternoon, and the school band will play live music near the pier for everyone who stays.

If it rains heavily, the event will not be cancelled completely. It will move to the following Sunday, and we will announce the change on the local radio. Please tell your neighbours and friends. A clean beach is a gift to every person and every animal that lives by the sea. Thank you for listening.

items.prompt: What is the topic of the workshop?
items.audio:
Good evening and welcome to our community garden workshop. My name is Farida Nazarova, and tonight I will show you how to make compost at home. Many families throw away nearly a third of their kitchen waste, but almost all of it can become rich soil for your plants, and it costs nothing.

First, you need a bin. You can buy one, but a wooden box or an old plastic barrel with holes in the sides works well. Put it in a sunny corner of your garden, directly on the ground, so that worms can come in from below. Worms are your best helpers.

Second, you need the right mixture. Compost needs two kinds of material. Green materials are wet and soft, for example vegetable peels, tea leaves and fresh grass. Brown materials are dry, for example fallen leaves, cardboard and egg boxes. The best mixture is one part green to two parts brown. If your compost smells bad, you probably have too much green. If it seems dry and nothing happens, add water and more vegetable waste.

Third, remember what not to add. Never put meat, fish, milk products or cooked food in the bin, because they smell and attract rats. Also avoid weeds with seeds, because the seeds will grow again in your garden.

Fourth, take care of the pile. Turn it with a fork every two weeks to bring air inside. The compost should be damp like a wrung sponge, not dry and not as wet as mud. In warm weather it will be ready in about four months. Good compost is dark, crumbly and smells like forest soil.

My neighbour, Mister Karim, started composting two years ago. He now uses it for his tomatoes, and he says they grow bigger and taste sweeter. He also stopped buying fertilizer, so he saves money. If you want a free bin from the city, please write your name on the list at the door. Our next workshop in October will be about growing herbs on a window sill. Thank you for coming.

items.prompt: Who presents the weather report?
items.audio:
Good evening, and welcome to the weather report for the Fergana Valley. I am Kamola Yusupova, and here is the forecast for the coming week.

Monday will be a bright and sunny day with a light breeze from the south. The temperature will reach twenty-eight degrees in the afternoon, so it is a perfect day for working outside. On Tuesday clouds will arrive from the west. The morning will stay dry, but a strong wind will begin at noon, and we expect light rain in the evening. Please take an umbrella if you will be out late.

Wednesday will be the most unpleasant day of the week. Thunderstorms are likely in the afternoon, and there will be heavy rain in the mountains. Rivers may rise quickly, so drivers and farmers should be careful near bridges and canals. The temperature will drop to eighteen degrees, and the evening will feel quite cold.

On Thursday the morning will begin with thick fog in the valley, and it will last until about ten o'clock. Drivers should use their lights and slow down. After that the sky will clear, and the afternoon will be calm and pleasant, with sunshine and light wind.

Friday will be warm and mostly sunny, with a temperature of twenty-four degrees. Gardeners can enjoy the day, because the ground will still be wet after the earlier rain and the plants will grow well.

Now to the weekend. Saturday will be very hot, with a temperature of thirty-three degrees and almost no clouds. The sun will be very strong around midday, so please wear a hat, stay in the shade if you can, and drink plenty of water. Parents should keep small children indoors during the hottest hours. On Sunday a dusty wind from the desert is possible, and the air may feel dry. People with breathing problems should be careful and stay at home when the dust is thick.

That is all for the weather. Thank you for listening, and have a good evening.

items.prompt: For how long has Anvar been a farmer?
items.audio:
In this interview, a journalist named Sevara talks to Anvar Rakhimov, a farmer from the Jizzakh region. Sevara asks him how this summer has been. Anvar sighs and says it has been the driest he can remember. He has grown cotton and wheat for thirty years, and he has never seen so little water. There was no rain at all for seventy days, and the main canal that brings water from the mountains was half empty in July.

Sevara asks what the drought did to his crops. Anvar explains that the wheat was not too bad, because it grows in spring when there is still some moisture in the ground. The cotton suffered more, and he thinks the harvest will be a quarter smaller than last year. Some of his neighbours lost their whole vegetable gardens.

However, Anvar was better prepared than many farmers. Two years ago he changed to drip irrigation, which brings small amounts of water directly to the roots of each plant through thin pipes. At first it was expensive, but now he uses forty percent less water than before, and the plants are healthier. He also chose a new kind of wheat that needs less water, and he built a large tank behind the house to collect rain in the few days when it does fall.

Sevara asks where he learned about these methods. Anvar smiles and says that his son Jasur, who studies agriculture in Tashkent, explained them. Jasur also taught him to use a phone application that measures the moisture of the soil, so he no longer waters the fields by guess.

Finally, Sevara asks what advice he would give to other farmers. Anvar says that the best time to water is early in the morning, before the sun is strong, because less water disappears into the air. He adds that the government gave him a loan to buy the pipes, and he hopes other farmers will receive the same help. He looks at the sky every evening and hopes for rain in autumn.

items.prompt: How did the penguins arrive at the zoo?
items.audio:
Welcome to Riverside Zoo, and thank you for visiting us today. We have some exciting news for all our guests. Last Tuesday, eight penguins arrived at the zoo by plane. They travelled for fourteen hours in special boxes, and they are now living in our brand new Penguin House, next to the elephant garden.

The penguins come from a colder part of the world, so we have made their home as natural as possible. The pool is kept at fourteen degrees, which is cold for people but perfect for penguins. The floor is covered with white stones and small rocks, and there is a wall of ice where they like to rest. Our zookeeper, Olga Sidorova, takes care of them every day. She says the birds are shy, and they spent the first three days staying close together, but now they are swimming happily and playing with each other.

You can see the penguins being fed twice a day, at eleven in the morning and at three in the afternoon. Each penguin eats about twenty small fish a day. Olga will talk about their habits at each feeding and will answer your questions, so please come early to find a good place near the glass.

We ask all visitors to follow a few simple rules. Please do not use flash when you take photographs, because the bright light can hurt the animals' eyes. Do not tap on the glass, and do not throw food into the water. Penguins can become ill if they eat the wrong things. Please keep your voice quiet in the Penguin House, so that the birds feel safe.

We also have a surprise for the spring. One of the female penguins has made a nest, and we hope that the first baby chick will be born in April. Children can help us choose a name by writing on the board near the exit.

Our opening hours are from nine in the morning to six in the evening. Children under five can enter for free. Enjoy your visit!

items.prompt: What is Botir Hamidov's job?
items.audio:
Thank you all for coming to this evening's talk. My name is Botir Hamidov, and I am an engineer. Tonight I want to tell you about the village of Oqtepa, high in the hills, where the sun has changed daily life.

Until two years ago, Oqtepa had no regular electricity. The only power came from an old diesel generator that was noisy, dirty and expensive. The fuel had to be carried by truck over a bad road, and when the road was blocked by snow, the village had no light at all. The generator worked for only four hours every evening.

Then a small project began. Last year, engineers installed thirty solar panels on the roofs of the school and the health clinic. The money was shared between an international fund and the villagers, who each paid a small part. The panels collect energy from the sun during the day, and big batteries store it, so that the lights and machines can work at night too.

The results were quick. At the clinic, a special refrigerator now keeps vaccines cold every day, so the nurse no longer needs to travel to the town to collect medicine. At the school, children use computers and read under bright lamps in the evening. Families spend less money on fuel, and the village is much quieter, because the generator is switched off.

Solar energy also needs care. The panels collect a lot of dust, so two young men from the village clean them every month. They learned this work in a short training course. In winter the panels give less power, because the days are shorter and cloudier, but the batteries are large enough for most needs.

The villagers are now planning the next step. Next year they want to install street lights along the main road, so that people can walk safely after dark. I believe this small village shows that clean energy is not only for rich cities. Thank you, and I am happy to answer your questions.

items.prompt: What is the name of the dog?
items.audio:
On Wednesday morning, Malika called the animal shelter in her town. She was very upset, and her voice was shaking. She explained to the worker, Jamshid, that her dog Bobo had disappeared the night before. Jamshid asks her to describe the dog. Malika answers that Bobo is a medium brown dog about three years old, with one white front paw and a red collar. He is friendly but also very nervous.

Jamshid asks what happened. Malika says that on Tuesday night there was a terrible thunderstorm with strong wind and heavy rain. Bobo was sleeping in the garden, but when the first loud thunder came, he jumped over the low fence and ran away into the darkness. Malika looked for him with a torch until midnight, but she could not find him. Jamshid says this is quite common, because many dogs are afraid of thunder and run far away when they are frightened.

Malika asks whether any brown dog has been brought to the shelter. Jamshid checks his list and says that a farmer brought in a similar dog yesterday afternoon, but it is bigger and has no collar. Malika thinks it is not Bobo, but she agrees to come and look at the dog after lunch. Jamshid also asks if Bobo has a microchip. Malika says yes, and the vet put it in last year, so Jamshid promises to check every dog with a special reader.

Then Jamshid gives Malika some useful tips. First, she should put an old blanket or a piece of her clothing outside the gate, because the smell of home can help the dog find his way back. Second, she should walk near the lake at dawn and call Bobo in a calm voice, because frightened dogs often hide in quiet places. Third, she should put a poster with his photograph on the trees in the neighbourhood.

Malika thanks him warmly. She does everything he said, and two days later a fisherman found Bobo under the old bridge near the lake. He was wet, tired and hungry, but unhurt.

items.prompt: What percentage of land do rainforests cover?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, class. Today we are going to talk about one of the most important places on our planet, the tropical rainforest. Please listen carefully, because next week there will be a short test.

Rainforests cover only about six percent of the land on Earth, but they are home to more than half of all the kinds of plants and animals in the world. The biggest one is in South America, around the Amazon River. It is almost as large as the whole of Europe.

A rainforest has four layers. The highest layer is called the emergent layer, where a few giant trees rise above everything else and where eagles build their nests. Below that is the canopy, a thick roof of leaves and branches. The canopy is so dense that only about two percent of the sunlight reaches the ground. Most of the animals, such as monkeys, parrots and tree frogs, live there. The third layer is the understory, which is dark and humid, and the lowest layer is the forest floor, where fallen leaves quickly turn into soil.

Rainforests are very wet. In some places more than two metres of rain falls every year. The trees release water into the air, and this creates clouds and rain, so the forest almost makes its own weather. Animals have clever ways to live there. The sloth, for example, moves very slowly, and green plants grow on its fur, which helps it hide from enemies.

Unfortunately, rainforests are in danger. People cut down trees for wood, farms and roads. Experts say that a piece of forest the size of a football pitch disappears every six seconds. This is a big problem, because a quarter of modern medicines come from rainforest plants, and because the trees take carbon dioxide out of the air.

So what can we do? We can buy recycled paper, avoid products made with cheap palm oil, and support groups that protect the forest. Indigenous people who live in the rainforest also protect it very well, and we should listen to them. Does anyone have any questions?
