items.prompt: Where does Aisha work?
items.audio:
Welcome back to our science podcast. Today I am talking to Doctor Aisha Rahman, a marine biologist who has spent twelve summers protecting sea turtles on the coast of Cyprus. Aisha, thank you for joining us.

Aisha begins by explaining something amazing. A female green turtle returns to lay her eggs on the same beach where she was born, even though she may have swum thousands of kilometres and spent about thirty years in the ocean. At night she crawls up the sand, digs a hole and lays about one hundred eggs. Then she covers them and goes back to the sea without ever seeing her babies.

I asked her how the babies are born. Aisha says that after about two months, the baby turtles break their shells and climb out of the sand, usually at night. They then run toward the sea. The most unusual fact is that the temperature of the sand decides whether the babies are male or female. Warm sand produces more females. Because the climate is getting hotter, some beaches now produce almost no males, and this is a serious worry for scientists.

Life is dangerous for hatchlings. Birds, crabs and fish eat many of them, and only one in a thousand survives to become an adult. Humans make things worse. Bright white lights from hotels confuse the babies, which walk toward the road instead of the water. Plastic bags look like jellyfish, and turtles eat them and become sick.

Aisha's team tries to help in several ways. They walk the beach at night with red lights, which do not confuse the turtles. They put cages over nests to protect them from foxes, and they have tagged forty turtles to learn where they travel. The nesting season lasts from June to August, and tourists can join guided night walks if they stay far from the animals and use no flash.

At the end I asked Aisha what gives her hope. She says it is the children who come to watch the hatchlings. She believes that a child who has seen a baby turtle reach the sea will protect nature for life.

items.prompt: How many trees do the volunteers plan to plant?
items.audio:
Good evening, neighbours. This is an announcement from the Green Yangiyul group about our big tree planting day, which will take place on the third Saturday of October. We would like to invite every family in our district to take part.

This year our goal is to plant two thousand young trees on the bare hill behind the old factory. For many years the hill has had almost no plants, and in heavy rain the soil slides down onto the road and into the gardens below. Trees have strong roots that hold the soil, so planting them is the best way to stop this problem. They will also give shade in summer and make the air cleaner. Scientists say that a district with many trees can be up to three degrees cooler during a hot summer.

We will plant three kinds of trees: pine, apple and walnut. The pines are good for the steep part of the hill, while the apples and walnuts will give fruit for children and birds in the future. All the saplings are a gift from the nursery of Mister Olimov, who has grown young trees for twenty-five years and wants to support our project.

Please meet at nine in the morning at the bus stop near the factory gate. Tools will be provided, and experts will show you how deep to dig and how to place the roots. Please wear strong boots and old clothes, and bring a hat. Hot tea and bread will be free for everyone at the break.

Every child who takes part may choose a tree and give it a name. We will attach a small wooden plaque with the name, so that in ten years a grown-up can come back and see how their tree has grown. A tree needs water, so volunteers will visit the hill every Sunday morning during the first month to water the saplings.

If you would like to join us, please sign up at the library by Thursday, so that we know how many tools and cups of tea to prepare. Thank you, and let us make our hill green again.

items.prompt: Who gave Dilnoza the idea for the reunion?
items.audio:
Good morning, listeners, and welcome to the weekend family programme. Today we are talking about family reunions, and we begin with a story from a listener called Dilnoza, who lives in Samarkand. Last summer she organised a reunion for her whole family, and she has kindly sent us the details.

Dilnoza says the idea came from her grandfather, Rustam, who turned eighty in June. He told her that he had not seen some of his cousins for more than twenty years, because they had moved to different countries. Dilnoza decided to find everyone and invite them. It took her three months, because she had to write letters, make phone calls and even ask old neighbours for addresses. In the end she found forty relatives, and thirty-two of them said they could come.

The reunion took place on the second Saturday of August in her aunt's large garden, which has apple trees and a long wooden table. The guests began arriving at ten in the morning. Some came by train from Tashkent, and two cousins even flew from Moscow. Dilnoza says the most emotional moment was when her grandfather met his younger sister, Gulbahor, who had lived in Kazakhstan since nineteen ninety. They simply held hands and did not speak for almost a minute.

For lunch, the women of the family cooked a huge pot of plov, and the men prepared kebabs. Children played football on the grass while the older guests looked through old photo albums. Dilnoza had also asked everybody to bring one photograph from their childhood, and by the afternoon they had made a family wall with more than one hundred pictures.

In the evening, her uncle Farhod, who plays the dutar, led the singing, and everyone danced until nearly midnight. Before leaving, the relatives agreed to meet again every two years, and next time the reunion will be in Bukhara.

Dilnoza ends her message with some advice. She says you should start planning early, choose a place with enough shade, and never forget to take a group photograph. Thank you, Dilnoza, and now let us hear some music.

items.prompt: When does the opening ceremony start?
items.audio:
Attention, please, all students, parents and teachers of Green Valley School. This is an important announcement from the head teacher, Mrs Karimova, about the start of the new school year.

First, the new term will begin on the first Monday of September. Students must arrive at the main gate before eight in the morning, because the opening ceremony starts at eight fifteen. It will take place in the sports hall, and it will last about forty minutes. Parents are warmly invited to attend, but please arrive early, because there are only two hundred seats.

Second, there are several changes this year. The school has built a new science laboratory on the second floor, and it is ready for use. Students in grades eight and nine will have chemistry lessons there every Tuesday and Thursday. The library has also been repaired. It now has a quiet reading room and thirty new computers, and it will stay open until five in the afternoon, one hour later than last year.

Third, the timetable. Lessons will start at eight thirty and finish at two fifteen. The lunch break lasts forty-five minutes, and the canteen will offer a new healthy menu with soup, fresh salad and fruit. Students who bring their own lunch may eat it in the garden if the weather is good.

Fourth, we have two new teachers joining us. Mr Alisher Tursunov will teach English and drama, and Miss Sarah Bennett, who comes from Manchester, will help older students prepare for international exams. We hope everyone will welcome them warmly.

Finally, a few reminders for parents. Every student needs a uniform, a school diary and a blue folder for homework. The uniform shop near the post office is open every day from nine until six, and it will give a ten percent discount during the first week. If your child has any health problems, please speak to our nurse, Mrs Yusupova, before the end of the first week.

The whole staff wishes you a happy, healthy and successful year. We look forward to seeing you all on the first day. Thank you for listening.

items.prompt: How long does the tour last?
items.audio:
Welcome to the City History Museum. My name is Madina, and I will be your guide this morning. Our tour lasts about one hour, and it will take us through the story of the Silk Road, the ancient network of trade routes that connected East and West.

Let us begin in this first hall. The Silk Road was not one single road, but many paths across deserts, mountains and rivers. It got its name from silk, which merchants carried from China to Europe. However, silk was only one of many goods. Traders also moved spices, glass, paper, horses, gold and even ideas. Notice the large map on the wall. The red line shows the main route, which began in Xi'an and ended in cities on the Mediterranean Sea. Our own region was right in the middle, and that is why cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara became so rich.

In the next hall you can see a caravan. A caravan was a group of merchants travelling together with camels. A camel could carry about two hundred kilograms and walk for many days without water. Journeys were long and dangerous. A trader might spend two years travelling from one end of the route to the other. Because of this, merchants rarely travelled the whole way. Instead, they sold their goods to another trader at a market town, and the goods moved slowly from hand to hand.

Now please follow me to the glass cases on your left. Here we have some of the museum's most precious objects: a blue ceramic bowl from the twelfth century, a bronze lamp and some old coins from many different countries. Archaeologists found them near the old city wall, about ten years ago.

Finally, in the last room you can try writing your name on handmade paper, just as scribes did centuries ago. Paper making came from China, and it changed the way people kept knowledge.

Before we begin, a few rules. Please do not touch the objects, and photography is allowed without a flash. If you have questions, just raise your hand. Shall we start?

items.prompt: Where did archaeologists find the objects?
items.audio:
Welcome to the City History Museum. My name is Madina, and I will be your guide this morning. Our tour lasts about one hour, and it will take us through the story of the Silk Road, the ancient network of trade routes that connected East and West.

Let us begin in this first hall. The Silk Road was not one single road, but many paths across deserts, mountains and rivers. It got its name from silk, which merchants carried from China to Europe. However, silk was only one of many goods. Traders also moved spices, glass, paper, horses, gold and even ideas. Notice the large map on the wall. The red line shows the main route, which began in Xi'an and ended in cities on the Mediterranean Sea. Our own region was right in the middle, and that is why cities such as Samarkand and Bukhara became so rich.

In the next hall you can see a caravan. A caravan was a group of merchants travelling together with camels. A camel could carry about two hundred kilograms and walk for many days without water. Journeys were long and dangerous. A trader might spend two years travelling from one end of the route to the other. Because of this, merchants rarely travelled the whole way. Instead, they sold their goods to another trader at a market town, and the goods moved slowly from hand to hand.

items.prompt: Where does Mrs Nazarova live now?
items.audio:
Hello, and welcome to our series called Voices of the Past. Today our reporter, Jasmine, is talking to Mrs Zulfiya Nazarova, who is eighty-one years old and lives in a small house in Namangan. Here is the interview, told in prose.

Jasmine begins by asking about her childhood. Mrs Nazarova answers that she was born in nineteen forty-five, in a village near the river. Her family was big, with seven children, and they all slept in one room. Life was simple, and there was no electricity in the village until she was twelve. In the evenings they used oil lamps, and her mother told stories while the children did their homework.

Jasmine then asks about school. Mrs Nazarova smiles and says that she walked five kilometres to school every day, even in winter. Her favourite subject was geography, because she loved learning about faraway places. Her teacher, Mr Aliev, was very strict, but he lent her books from his own shelf. She still remembers the first book she read, which was about explorers in the Arctic.

Next, Jasmine asks about work. After school Mrs Nazarova trained as a nurse, and she worked in the same hospital for thirty-eight years. She says it was hard work, with long night shifts, but she felt proud to help people. She met her husband, Karim, at the hospital, when he came as a patient with a broken leg. They married two years later and had three children.

Jasmine asks what has changed most in her lifetime. Mrs Nazarova thinks for a moment and says that it is communication. When she was young, a letter took two weeks to arrive. Now she can see her grandchildren in Germany on a small screen every Sunday. She laughs and adds that she prefers letters, but she has to admit that video calls are wonderful.

Finally, Jasmine asks for her advice to young people. Mrs Nazarova says, be kind, work hard and never stop learning. Thank you, Mrs Nazarova, for sharing your memories with us.

items.prompt: When will the new tram line open?
items.audio:
Good afternoon, citizens. This is a public announcement from the City Transport Department about an exciting new project: the opening of tram line number four.

After two years of construction, the new tram line will open on the fifteenth of October. The line is eleven kilometres long, and it connects the main railway station with the university district in the north of the city. There are fourteen stops along the route, including the central market, the national library and the large park near the river. The journey from end to end takes twenty-six minutes, which is almost half the time of the bus.

The trams themselves are modern and comfortable. Each one is thirty metres long, has air conditioning and can carry two hundred and ten passengers. There are free wireless internet connections, charging points for phones and special places for wheelchairs and baby carriages. Because the trams run on electricity, they produce no smoke, and the city hopes that the new line will reduce traffic by about fifteen percent.

Now, some practical information. Trams will run every seven minutes during the day and every fifteen minutes in the evening. The first tram leaves the station at five thirty in the morning, and the last one at eleven at night. A single ticket costs two thousand five hundred som, and you can pay by card or with the city travel app. Students and pensioners get a fifty percent discount, and children under seven travel for free. items.prompt: What does Behzod want to study?
items.audio:
This is a story about a phone call between a student called Behzod and the admissions office of a university in Tashkent. Listen carefully and think about what advice you would give him.

Behzod is eighteen, and he has just finished school with very good marks. He wants to study computer science, but he is not sure how to apply, so he calls the university on a Monday morning. A friendly woman named Mrs Ismoilova answers the phone.

Behzod asks when the application period starts. Mrs Ismoilova explains that students can apply from the first of June until the thirty-first of July. He asks what documents he needs. She says he must bring his school certificate, a copy of his passport, six small photographs and a medical certificate. If he has any language certificates, such as an English test result, he should bring those too, because they can give him extra points.

Next Behzod asks about the entrance exam. Mrs Ismoilova tells him that it has three parts: mathematics, physics and English. The exam lasts three hours, and it takes place in the main building on the fifth of August. Applicants who score above seventy percent receive a place on the budget, which means they do not pay for their studies. The others can still study, but they must pay a yearly fee of about eight million som.

Behzod is a little worried about the cost, so he asks about scholarships. Mrs Ismoilova says that there are two kinds. One is for students with the best exam results, and the other is for students from families with a low income. He can find the full details on the university website, in a section called Student Support.

Finally, Behzod asks whether he can visit the campus before applying. She answers that open days take place every Saturday in May, and guides will show visitors the lecture halls, the laboratories and the dormitory. Behzod thanks her, writes down the information, and decides to come on the next Saturday.

items.prompt: What does Navruz mean?
items.audio:
Hello, everyone, and welcome to our cultural talk. This week we celebrate Navruz, the spring festival, and I would like to tell you about how the holiday is celebrated in our city.

Navruz means new day in Persian, and it marks the beginning of spring. It takes place on the twenty-first of March, when day and night are exactly equal in length. People have celebrated this holiday for more than three thousand years, and today it is enjoyed by millions of people in many countries across Asia.

Preparations begin weeks before the holiday. Families clean their houses, repay old debts and forgive old arguments, because the new year should start with a fresh heart. Children plant wheat seeds in small dishes, and by the day of the festival the green shoots are about ten centimetres tall. This dish of green wheat is called sumalak when it is cooked, and the women prepare it together during a long night. They stir a huge pot for almost twenty-four hours, singing songs and telling stories. According to tradition, nobody sleeps during that night, and everyone makes a wish.

On the day of the festival, the main square of our city is full of life. There are concerts, folk dances and traditional sports. Horse games, such as kupkari, attract large crowds, and wrestlers compete for a prize of a sheep. Along the streets, craftsmen sell pottery, carpets and wooden toys, and food stalls offer pilaf, samsa and sweets. Last year, more than fifty thousand visitors came to the square, and the organisers expect even more this year.

Families also visit each other. Guests bring small gifts, and the host must offer a table full of food. It is said that the more generous the table, the happier the year will be. Children receive coins and sweets, and older people give blessings.

Navruz is not only a celebration of nature, but also a time of kindness, friendship and hope. I wish you all a peaceful and happy Navruz. Now, let us listen to a traditional song.

items.prompt: When was the library founded?
items.audio:
Welcome back to our morning programme. Today we are visiting the Central City Library, and we are speaking with the head librarian, Mr Otabek Rahimov. Here is a summary of our conversation.

Our presenter, Laura, begins by asking how long the library has existed. Mr Rahimov explains that it was founded in nineteen twenty-six, with just two thousand books in a small room above a bakery. Today the collection has almost one million books, magazines and old newspapers, and it occupies a large building with five floors.

Laura asks what a typical day looks like. Mr Rahimov laughs and says that no day is typical. He arrives at seven thirty, checks the mail and meets his team of twenty-two employees. The library opens at nine, and by ten there is usually a queue of students waiting for the reading room. In the afternoon, there are workshops for children, and in the evening the library hosts book clubs and language classes.

Next Laura asks about the changes brought by technology. Mr Rahimov says that many people believe libraries are disappearing, but the opposite is true. The number of visitors has grown by thirty percent in the last five years. Readers can now borrow electronic books, listen to audiobooks and use free computers. However, he adds that paper books remain very popular, especially among teenagers, who enjoy fantasy and adventure novels.

Laura then asks about the most valuable item in the collection. He answers that it is a handwritten manuscript from the fourteenth century, which contains poems and medical advice. It is kept in a special room with a controlled temperature, and visitors may see it only with permission. He adds that the library is now scanning old manuscripts so that people around the world can read them online.

Finally, Laura asks what advice he would give to someone who does not like reading. Mr Rahimov smiles and says that you should just find the right book. Start with a subject you love, read ten pages every evening, and soon it will become a pleasant habit.

Thank you, Mr Rahimov, for your time.

items.prompt: What does the word Registan mean?
items.audio:
Good morning, everyone, and thank you for joining this lecture about one of the most famous squares in Central Asia, the Registan in Samarkand. My name is Professor Aziza Mirzaeva, and for the next forty minutes I will take you on a journey through its history.

The word Registan means sandy place in Persian. In the Middle Ages, it was an open area covered with sand, where people gathered to hear royal announcements, watch public events and trade goods. At that time there were no grand buildings, only simple shops and a small market.

The story of the great buildings began in the fifteenth century, during the rule of Ulugh Beg, the grandson of Timur. Ulugh Beg was not only a ruler but also a famous astronomer and mathematician. In fourteen twenty, he built a madrasa on the western side of the square, and it became one of the best schools in the Muslim world. Students came from many countries to study mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy. The building has a beautiful blue tiled entrance and two tall minarets.

Two centuries later, a governor named Yalangtush Bahodur decided to add two more buildings. The first, the Sher-Dor madrasa, was completed in sixteen thirty-six. It is famous for the pictures of tigers, or more exactly lions, chasing deer on its main arch, which is unusual because Islamic art rarely shows animals. The second building, the Tilya-Kori madrasa, was finished in sixteen sixty. Its name means covered with gold, and the inside of its mosque is decorated with thousands of gold leaves.

Over the centuries the buildings suffered from earthquakes and neglect. By the nineteenth century, some walls were close to collapse. Restoration began in the twentieth century and continues to this day. In two thousand one, the Registan became part of the UNESCO World Heritage list.

Today the square welcomes about two million visitors a year. In the evenings, lights and music transform the buildings into a magical show. When you visit, I advise you to arrive at sunset, when the tiles shine most brightly. Now, are there any questions?

items.prompt: Where does Malika study?
items.audio:
This is a story about a phone call between two sisters, Nilufar and Malika. Nilufar lives in Tashkent, and Malika studies in London. They talk every Sunday evening, and this week the conversation was about food.

Nilufar starts by saying that she has had a wonderful weekend. On Saturday she went to visit their grandmother, Oyi, in her old house, and they spent the whole day cooking together. Oyi wanted to teach her the recipe for manti, the steamed dumplings that Malika loves so much.

Malika asks how it went. Nilufar laughs and says that it was harder than she expected. First, they made the dough with flour, water, salt and a little oil. Oyi told her that the dough must rest for thirty minutes, and she should never hurry. Then they prepared the filling with lamb, onions and pumpkin. Nilufar had to cut the onions, and she cried like a child, which made her grandmother laugh.

The most difficult part was shaping the dumplings. Oyi can make a perfect manti in just a few seconds, but Nilufar needed almost five minutes for the first one. By the end of the afternoon they had made sixty, and Nilufar says that her last ones looked quite good. They steamed them for forty minutes and ate them with yoghurt and fresh dill.

Malika says that she is a little jealous, because in London she cannot find a good restaurant for Uzbek food. Nilufar promises to write down the recipe and send it by email. She adds that Oyi also told her stories about her own childhood, when she cooked on an open fire for ten brothers and sisters. Nilufar felt that these stories were as important as the recipe.

They decide that when Malika comes home in July, the three of them will cook together again. This time Malika will make the dough, Nilufar will prepare the filling, and Oyi will show them how to be patient. Malika says that she cannot wait, and they say goodnight.

Nilufar starts by saying that she has had a wonderful weekend. On Saturday she went to visit their grandmother, Oyi, in her old house, and they spent the whole day cooking together. Oyi wanted to teach her the recipe for manti, the steamed dumplings that Malika loves so much.

Malika asks how it went. Nilufar laughs and says that it was harder than she expected. First, they made the dough with flour, water, salt and a little oil. Oyi told her that the dough must rest for thirty minutes, and she should never hurry. Then they prepared the filling with lamb, onions and pumpkin. Nilufar had to cut the onions, and she cried like a child, which made her grandmother laugh.

The most difficult part was shaping the dumplings. Oyi can make a perfect manti in just a few seconds, but Nilufar needed almost five minutes for the first one. By the end of the afternoon they had made sixty, and Nilufar says that her last ones looked quite good. They steamed them for forty minutes and ate them with yoghurt and fresh dill.

Malika says that she is a little jealous, because in London she cannot find a good restaurant for Uzbek food. Nilufar promises to write down the recipe and send it by email. She adds that Oyi also told her stories about her own childhood, when she cooked on an open fire for ten brothers and sisters. Nilufar felt that these stories were as important as the recipe.

They decide that when Malika comes home in July, the three of them will cook together again. This time Malika will make the dough, Nilufar will prepare the filling, and Oyi will show them how to be patient. Malika says that she cannot wait, and they say goodnight.

items.prompt: When will Clean Park Day take place?
items.answer: On the last Saturday of April
items.audio:
Hello, neighbours, and welcome to this week's community radio news. We begin with an announcement about a big event for the whole city: the annual Clean Park Day.

This year the event will take place on the last Saturday of April at the Youth Park, which is the largest green area in our district. The organisers, a local group called Green Hands, are looking for at least five hundred volunteers. Last year only three hundred people came, but they collected an incredible two tonnes of rubbish in just four hours.

The programme is as follows. Volunteers should meet at the main entrance at nine in the morning, where they will get gloves, bags and a bright yellow vest. The organisers will divide everyone into groups of ten, and each group will clean a different part of the park. There are five zones: the lake, the playground, the forest path, the football field and the picnic area. At twelve there will be a short break, with free tea, bread and fruit for everyone. The work will end at one in the afternoon.

After the clean-up, there will be some fun activities. Children can paint pictures on stones, which will be placed along the paths, and a local band will play music near the lake. At two o'clock, the mayor, Mr Sardor Aminov, will plant a young oak tree to mark the day. In addition, the city has promised to plant fifty new trees this spring and install twenty new benches and ten bins.

The leader of Green Hands, a young woman named Kamola, says that the aim is not only to clean but also to change people's habits. She asks everyone to take their rubbish home after a picnic and to use fewer plastic bags. She also reminds parents that children under twelve must come with an adult.

To register, send a message through the group's page or simply come on the day. Wear comfortable shoes and old clothes, and bring a bottle of water. Let us make our city cleaner together. Now, the weather report.
options: On the first Saturday of April

items.prompt: How long did Mr Qodirov teach?
items.audio:
Good evening, and welcome to our programme about people who make a difference. Tonight we tell the story of Mr Anvar Qodirov, a teacher who retired last month after forty-two years in the same school in Fergana.

Mr Qodirov was born in nineteen sixty-one in a family of farmers. As a boy, he did not plan to become a teacher. He wanted to be an engineer and build bridges. But in his last year at school, a history teacher called Mrs Saidova noticed his talent for explaining things to other students, and she suggested that he should think about teaching. He followed her advice, studied at the pedagogical institute in Tashkent, and in nineteen eighty-four he started work in a small school near his home town.

Over the years he taught history, geography and, for a short time, even physical education. He says his first class was terrifying. There were thirty-five students, and some of them were only three years younger than he was. However, he soon discovered that the secret of good teaching was to listen. He asked students questions, let them argue, and used stories instead of dates to make history alive.

His students describe him as patient and funny. One former student, now a doctor, says that Mr Qodirov once took the whole class to a village to meet an old man who remembered the war. That meeting, she says, taught her more than any textbook. Another student, now an engineer, laughs and says that his teacher was proud of him even though he never became a historian.

During his career, Mr Qodirov received three national awards, but he says that his greatest reward is meeting former students in the street. He estimates that he has taught more than two thousand people.

Now that he is retired, he plans to write a book about local history and to spend more time with his five grandchildren. He also wants to learn to play the piano. His advice for young teachers is simple: love your subject, respect your students, and never stop being curious. Thank you for listening.

items.prompt: When does the market close?
items.audio:
Hello, and welcome to our weekend guide to city life. Today we are visiting a place that comes alive after dark: the Night Market of Chilanzar. I walked there last Friday with my friend Sevara, and I would like to tell you about our evening.

The market opens at six in the evening and closes at one in the morning. It is held on the long street behind the old cinema, and it has more than two hundred stalls. When we arrived, the air was already full of delicious smells, and thousands of small lights hung above the street. Music came from every corner, and street performers juggled and played guitars.

First, we looked at the clothes and accessories. Sevara bought a handmade leather bag for about one hundred and twenty thousand som, after a friendly discussion about the price. The seller, an old man called Mr Hakim, told us that he had made bags for thirty years and that his father had taught him the craft. I bought a pair of silver earrings for my mother, whose birthday is next week.

Then we went to the food section, which is the heart of the market. There were dozens of choices. We tried grilled fish, fried dumplings and a sweet dish made of pumpkin and nuts. Sevara said that the best thing was a hot corn drink, which cost only five thousand som. We sat at a small plastic table, watched the crowd and talked for almost an hour.

After dinner, we visited the book corner, where students sell second-hand books at very low prices. I found an old atlas for ten thousand som. Near the exit there was a small stage, where a group of young people performed a comedy show. The audience laughed so loudly that we could hear them from the other end of the street.

We left at about eleven and took a taxi home. My advice is to go early, because it becomes crowded after eight, and to bring cash, since not all stalls accept cards. Next week, we will visit the old town. Until then, enjoy your weekend.

items.prompt: How many years ago did the centre open?
items.audio:
Welcome, everyone, and thank you for coming to the open day of the Bright Future Language Centre. My name is Sherzod, and I am the director of studies. In the next few minutes I would like to tell you about our school, our courses and our teachers.

Our centre opened eight years ago with only twelve students and two classrooms. Today we have more than nine hundred students, aged from six to sixty, and four branches in different parts of the city. We teach English, German, Korean and Turkish, but English is still our most popular language, with about sixty percent of all students.

Let me explain how our courses work. Every new student takes a short test and a speaking interview, so that we can find the right level. There are six levels, from beginner to advanced. Each course lasts three months, and classes meet three times a week for ninety minutes. We keep our groups small, with a maximum of twelve students, so that everyone has a chance to speak. Beginners often tell us that they are afraid to make mistakes, but our teachers create a friendly atmosphere where mistakes are a natural part of learning.

We also offer special courses. For example, there is an exam preparation course for students who want to take international tests, and a business English course for people who work in offices. This summer we are starting a new programme for teenagers, which combines language lessons with sport and drama. It will run for six weeks in July and August.

About our teachers: sixteen of them are local specialists with university degrees, and six are native speakers from Britain, America and Australia. All of them take part in training every month.

Finally, the prices. A three-month course costs one million two hundred thousand som, but today only, anyone who registers will receive a twenty percent discount and a free notebook. You can also try a free trial lesson next Wednesday at five. Please take a leaflet at the door, and do not hesitate to ask me any questions. Thank you.

items.prompt: What is the name of the play?
items.audio:
Hello, culture lovers, and welcome to our weekly arts review. This week I went to see a new play at the Navoi Theatre, and I would like to share my impressions with you.

The play is called The Last Train, and it was written by a young playwright from Tashkent named Ozoda Hamidova. It tells the story of a family in a small town in nineteen sixty, whose lives change when a new railway station opens. The main character is a grandmother called Hanifa, played by the experienced actress Mukhayyo Tursunova, and I must say that her performance was outstanding. She made the audience laugh in the first act and cry in the second.

The play lasts two hours and forty minutes, with one interval of twenty minutes. The set is simple but clever. A single wooden platform becomes a kitchen, a street and a train station, and the changes happen so quickly that you hardly notice them. The costumes are colourful and look authentic, and the music, performed live by a small group of three musicians, creates a warm atmosphere.

I have only two small complaints. First, the beginning is a little slow, and it takes almost twenty minutes for the real action to start. Second, some of the younger actors speak too quietly, and sitting at the back, I could not hear every word. But these are minor problems.

What I loved most was the message. The play shows how people can be afraid of change, but also how progress can bring families together. I left the theatre thinking about my own grandparents and the stories they told me. The audience, which was mostly families and students, stood and applauded for nearly five minutes.

If you would like to see it, there are performances every Friday and Saturday at seven in the evening until the end of next month. Tickets cost between forty and one hundred thousand som, and students pay half price. Book early, because the theatre has only four hundred seats, and the shows are almost sold out.

My rating is four and a half stars out of five. Join us next week, when we will talk about a new exhibition of modern art.
